summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31. 1965 and March 31st, 1967 respectively in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1 lakh on account of interest due on accrual basis. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interest on the money lending investments could not be included in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee. In doing so, the Appellate Tribunal followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth Tax officer applied under sub section (1) of section 27 of the Wealth Act for a reference of the cases to this Court in view of the conflict of opinion between the Orissa High Court and the Andhra Pradesh High Court, and so these references have been made. Under section 3 of the wealth Tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of an assessee on the corresponding valuation date. Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee on valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate value of all the debts owed by the assessee upon the valuation date; and (2) where an assessment is made in pursuance of section 19A, the valuation dates for the purposes of this Act shall be the same valuation date as would have been adopted in respect Of the net assets of the deceased if he were alive. The Wealth tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that accrued interest was liable to be included under the wealthtax assessments of an 'Hindu undivided Family. On appeal, the Tribunal held that accrued Interest was chargeable to wealth Tax for the Assessment years 1965 67 and 1966 68 (The respective valuation date being March31, 1965), in the hands of the Income tax Officer on the basis of cash system accounting the corresponding value dates being march 31, 1966 and March31. 1967 respectively. The High Court dismissed the reference holding that accrued interests were liable to included in wealth tax assessment of the respondent assessee. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: (1)(a) It is apparent from the definition or "net wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value". of all assets" belonging to an assessee under the Wealth tax Act, as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Commissioner of Wealth tax, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation day. All the assets of a assessee, bar those expressly excepted by the statute, are to be taken into account and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of Accounting or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accountancy adopted by the Income Tax Officer. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section(I) of s.7 as the estimate price which, according to the Wealthtax Officer, the assets would fetch, if sold, in open market, on the Valuation date. It is clear that what accrues as a right also falls to be excluded within the assets Of an assessee unders the WealthTax Act. That being so, even though the accounts of the assesee are maintained on cash basis interest due thereon, though not realised, on valuation the outstandings of the money lent business are liable to tax be included In the net income of the assesses. [310 G H] (b) It appears that what accrued as a rights also falls under the assessee under Wealth Tax Act.

The respondent was dismissed from service by the Central Administrative Tribunal, Chandigarh. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal on the ground that he had been convicted on a criminal charge. The High Court reversed this order on the view that if some but not all of t he findings of the enqui ry officer or the Tribunal prima facie make out a case of misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it was not for the appel lant to consider whether that ground alone would have weigh ed with the authority in imposing the penalty. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the order imposing a lesser penalty on the respondent, this Court, HELD: (1) In the case of proceedings transferr ed to the Tribunal from a civil court or High Court, the Tribu nal has the jurisdiction to exercise all the powers whi ch the civil court could in a suit or the High Courts in a proceeding could have respectively exercised. It will be open to the Government to decide whether, on the basis of the se charges, the punishment of dismissal should be maintain ed 'or else whether a lesser punishment would suffice for which t he penalty can lawfullybe imposed, and if so, what that penalty should be . . A government servant who is aggriev ed by the penalty imposed can agitate in appeal, revision or review as the case may be, that the penalty was too seve re or excessive and not warranted by the facts and circu stances of the case. If it is his case that he is not t he government servant, who has been in fact convicted, it wi ll strike down the impugned order and order him to be reinsta t ed in service. [319B C] (2) In view of the principles to which we have called attention and in view of th e aforesaid discussion, the ord er of the Tribunal imposing a higher penalty on t he respond ent cannot, therefore, be sustained. [520C D] (3) In Union of India vs Tulsiram Patel this Court set aside t he order of the Tribun al and ordered his reinstatement in service with fu ll back wages. The court can inste ad substitute a penalty which in its opinion would be just a nd proper in the circumstances of the ease. [620D] (4) In State of Orissa vs Bidyabhushan Mohapatra, ; , referred to.

The appellants were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff Inacio Martins who died pendente lite. He had filed a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No.1. The first ground on which the High Court dismissed the suit was that the suit had been barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. That suit, however, came to be dismissed as the Trial Court came to the conclusion that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the property in respect of which he claimed to be a lessee. It would have been a different matter if in the previous suit the court had decided the question of status as lessee against the plaintiff, in which case, perhaps it could be argued that the second suit based on the factum of tenancy was not maintainable. The High Court took the view that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of his land within the period allowed by section 18 of the Act and had, therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the suit property on the strength of his tenancy. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction is, therefore vested in the Mamlatdar under section 7 of the Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. [1032C] 2. In such a situation the Civil Court would not be competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant. [ 1034D] 3. Section 8(2) specifically bars the jurisdiction of all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the Act required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the Mamlatdar. The Jurisdiction of the Civil Courts stands wholly barred by virtue of section 58(2). [1034E] 4. In the instant case, the suit for possession was based on a distinct cause of action not found in the former Suit and hence it could not be said that the High court was right in concluding that the suits were barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [934F] 5. The question which arose in the suit being whether defendant No 1 was a tenant or a deemed tenant was required to he decided by the Civil court if the issue is held against defendant No1, the Civil Judge may consider passing of a decree in eviction but if on the other hand he is held to be tenant, the civil Court would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant is a trespasser.

The petitioners are carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the "Corpo ration"). They demand payment in terms paid to their counterparts in regular services. They want the same pay of the regular employees as carpenter or in the alternative, the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. The case of the Corporation is that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act. The Government has not fixed the mini mum wages payable to the petitioners engaged in the Corpora tion or other like industries but the Corporation has adopted the minimum wage payable for similar work in the construction industry. They are being paid the same wages as are payable to carpentars, painters and carpents ' helpers engaged in construction industry and abroad. The Corporation has clearly stated that there are no regular employees of the petitioners ' categories in its establishment and, as such, the question of payment to the peti tioners does not arise. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that the Corporation had reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. The Court, therefore, directed the Central Government to fix the pay scale of the petitioner on par with his counterparts doing similar work under the same employer. In the immediate aftermath of the decision in Randhir Singh case, there were bumper cases filed in this Court for enforcement of their right to have "equal pay for equal work". The Court pointed out that the principle of "equal Pay for equal Work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. It is, therefore not impermissible to provide two different pay scales in the same cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority.

The appellants were charged for the murder of one Malan, daughter of Kishan and accused 1 to 3 under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. on the allegation that in pursuance of the conspiracy and in furtherance of their common intention they committed the murder. The Sessions Judge acquitted all the seven accused but convicted them of the charge framed against them under section 120B I. P.C., and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life under section 304 read with s 34 I P. C. In appeal, the High Court held that the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against him in view of the fact that he was a party to charge No. 4 which was framed only against accused 1, 6 and 7. The High Court also rejected Criminal Appeal No. 287 of 1980 filed by the State for enhancement of the sentence of imprisonment awarded to accused 1 and 6 for the death of Malan under section 307 read with Section 34 IP. C., and confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to them. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The retracted judicial confessions of accused 4 could not have been relied upon in this case in view Of the fact, that accused 6 who had been tried alongwith accused 5 had been acquitted by the High court of the charges framed against him under section 148 read with sections 120B and 302 readwith s.120B I P P.c., and accused 5 was not charged for offence of murder of Malin beyond all reasonable doubt and that he had been rightly convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for death under s.302 read with S.34 I. PP.C.; (2) The confession of the accused 6 could not, therefore, be relied on against accused 6 in view o the fact the retracted confessional judicial confession was rightly convicted by the trial court and confirmed by the confirmation of the conviction of accused 6 by the Sessions Judge under section302 readwith section 34 Cr. P C., respectively. [138A B] (3) It is well settled that a retracted judicial statement can be relied only against an accused person who has been tried along with him in connection with the commission of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, but it cannot be used as evidence against him. [139F G] (4) The confessional statement of accused 1 could not therefore be relied against accused 5 in this context in view that he has been rightly acquitted by both the courts below.

The appellant was the sole executor of a will alleged to have been executed by one Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, (exhibit A) and he had stated that he prepared a draft at Mysore a day before the will was executed and that the will Was written in one room and Lakshmma was lying in the adjoining room and it was after the will had been written that the scribe went into the adjoining rooms and read the will to her so that the statement of the scribe that the testator was written in the presence of Lakshmabai is not supported by the appellant. The trial court held that the testatrix fully understood the contents of the will and put her signatures on it when she was in a sound and disposing state of mind, that he did not at all support the appellant 's case about previous instruction because, according to him, the testatrix said that she would agree to whatever the appellant would get written. The High Court further held that even if it had found in favour of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it was held that he had really understood its contents before he put her signature to the will, and since he had taken a leading part in its execution, the onus was heavy on him to remove the suspicions attending the execution of the document and to establish that Lakshmaiah had actually understood the nature and effect of the dispositions before she put her sign to the Will. Held: (i) The evidence of the attesting witness is clearly inconsistent with the appellant "s case regarding previous instructions and so it would be difficult to treat the evidence of this witness as suffi cient to prove that the propounder fully understood his contents, had approved of them and had put her initials on it while she was at a sound disposing state. (ii) The onus is heavy on the propounder to establish by satisfactory evidence that the Will was signed by the testator, that the executant at the relevant time was in sound and disposed state of minds, that it represented his intentions; and (iii) The propounder would be called upon to show by satisfactory proof that the document was read out fully to the testatrix and she understood the terms and conditions of its contents.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of Arc carbons, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons", manufactured by the appellant company. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether arc carbon manufactured by it could be covered by the entry under consideration. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the use of the term "electrode" to describe them, suggesting a connection with electricity, and (2) the Sales Tax authorities were compelled to consider the use which is generally made of the arc carcons under consideration, because of the use to which they are generally put. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The word "accessories" is used in several entries, such as entry No. Of course, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for use as an aid or addition. It will be noticed that the words "parts thereof" are used in various entries, but excludes certain other articles by putting in the words 'not being such articles as are ordinarily also used for other purposes than as (1 ) (1965) 16 S.T.C. (2)(1970) 26 S. T.C., (3) (1970) 27 S.S.T.,C. and excludes certain others by putting into the words `accessories ' which are required for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. It would be noticed from the fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. This finding was enough, in our opinion, to justify the view taken by the Andhra Pradesh High Court that the goods under consideration are covered by Entry No. 4 of Schedule 1 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1957, because they fall within the relevant entry 4 of the Schedule to the Mysore Sales Tax, Act, 1953, and exclude certain other items by putting In the words, "accessory" which are so very different and could have only a very remote hearing, if any, upon any reasoning which could be adopted to support the submission that the arc vehiclebons under Consideration here fall within this entry merely because a purchaser makes some other use of it. The fact that these are known as 'cinema arc carbolic goods ' in the market is evident from the facts that they cannot also be use for search purposes lights, signsalling stage lighting or where suitable lighting for photographsy or others may be needed, could no detract from their classification to that which the Carbon arcs belongs. [659 D] (b) The entry No 4 occurs in a schedule in which descriptions of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression 'accessories' has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. The first entry in the schedule relates to "motor vehicles" and includes "component parts of motor vehicles". It will, therefore, be clear that the term 'accessory ' is used as a part of a particular kind of apparatus, would not cease to be covered under the intended entry merely when a purchaser make some other uses of it, but exclude certain others from being such goods as are normally also use for other purpose than as "1) (1965), 16 S,T. C. (3). [660 G H] (c) The High Court correctly held that the main use of 'electrode ' to describe their goods, suggesting an connection with Electricity, or their utilisation in a process involving application of electrical power could convert them into "electrical goods" as contemplated by the Entry in the Madras Act.

Rule 21 of the Rules provides for the determination of the rate of royalty payable in respect of minor minerals. The original rule 21 was substituted by new rule 21 by the issue of impugned notification on 26 6 1985 which provided that a holder of a quarry lease or any other mineral conces sion granted under the Rules shall pay royalty at the rate prescribed for the time being in the rules framed by the State Government in respect thereof, removed or consumed by him or by his agent, manager, employee, contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the rates respectively specified against them in column 3 of the said Schedule. The rule also provides that no royalty shall be charged from Nimbhadas of village Potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year and by the village potters whose annual production was not exceeding two lakh bricks and who supply at least one lakh brick to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. Under Rule 18 of the rules the period of lease in the case of the minor minerals can be for a much longer period, it can be upto 10 years in respect o major minerals except in the cases of ordinary sand, Kankar, Murram and gravel a lease can be granted upto three years, and the area or land covered by a mining lease is governed by rule 15 which says that no quarry lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of specified minor mineral and 20 hec tares in the Case of other minerals. So a comparison of the relevant rules would show that a larger restriction was imposed both on the area in respect Of which a Parwana could be issued and the duration of the Parwana right and as also stated that the persons who take quarrying Parwana are persons belonging to the weaker sections of society and if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot be said that there is no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to Rule 21 to show concession in the matter of payment of royalty and the social policy underlying the Constitution, the statute and the Rules. The petitioners in some of the petitions had two contentions: 1. that the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose; and 2. that since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the state, the levy was bad; and 3. that there was no reasonable connection between the Classification for purposes o f proviso to rule 21 to showing concession in respect the matter o payment of royalties and the Social Policy underlying the constitution, the Act and the rules. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1(a) The impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. [419D] 2(b) The State Government is empowered to make rules for regulating the grant of quarry leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in re spect of minor Minerals and for purposes connected there with. Rule 18 provides for determination of rate of royalties payable in relation to minor minerals except under in accordance with rule 15, which says, that no quarrying lease shall he granted for any area exceeding ten hectares in cases where the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used only for development of minerals and not for other purpose sanctioned by law. The fact that section 15 of the Act does no authorise the State Govern ment to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. No express power need to conferred on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification for purpose of implementing the policy of the statute under which the Rules are made.

The appellant was the hereditary trustee of a temple. The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the Kumaran Koil was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of Madras Act 19 of 1951. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge Nagapattinam. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the succession was "regulated by usage"; (2) according to the usage of the temple the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meeting of the members of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so, the appellant must be held to be a trustee within section 6 (9) Of Act 19 Of 1951; (3) succession being specifically provided for by the founder on condition that the scheme of such succession is still in force; and (4) succession having to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. HELD: (1)(a) The office of a hereditary trustees is in the nature of property. It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is an vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. [446 D] (b) In the case of mutts, whose heads are often celibates and sometimes sanyasins, special rules of succession obtain by custom and usage. In Sital Das vs Sant Ram(5) the law was taken as well settled that succession to the mahantship of a mutt or religious institution is regulated by custom or usage. But the election to the office of trustee in the present case is for a fixed period of two years and not for life. It was, therefore, difficult to hold that the office could be said to be hereditary within the sense that on the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the Office as a matter of course because the successor acquires a right only 'by appointment and the authority to appoint is vested in the assembly of the bairagis and the worshippets.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the second accused, Jabamani Nadar alias Kanyakumari Comrade alias Ramu and also observed that necessarily no case would lie on this kind of testimony against even the absconding accused. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court 'can place no reliance on the testimony of PW 4 in so far as he implicated the second appellant and Tharnizarasan in the case of murder of Viswanatham. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court is not even right that PW 4 stands wholly corroborated by the contents of the FIR. On the other hand, it stands to reason that those persons who gathered would not ask PW 4, who arrived at the place a little later, for information with regard to the assailants. There is considerable doubt as to this testimony with regard regard to seeing the accused running away from the place where he was sleeping to the place of occurrence. When the accused is 712 going to lose his life in such a serious charge it is only necessary that the court should be circumspect and closely scrutinise the evidence to come to an unhesitating conclusion that he is absolutely reliable. [707B C] (2) The fact that the witness has stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the medical evidence. Another very serious departure from his earlier version is that while PW 4 had stated in his first information Report that "my elder brother" (meaning the deceased) was "chasing him from behind" in court he has completely given a go by to this statement and stated that Karunakaran was being chased by PWs 1, 2 and 3. If his statement in court that he saw PWs 1 , 2 and 4 chasing Karunakaran while running away after the assault is true, it is difficult to appreciate that he would not mention about this fact in the second information report. [807C D] (3) The evidence of PW4 stands contradicted by his testimony in court on a very material point. For the reasons given above we are unable to place such reliance as is requisite on the evidence of this solitary eye witness. It also stands to logic that those witnesses who gathered at the scene of occurrence a little earlier than PW 4 did not see the assailants who might have had escaped.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of one Amarchand N. Shroff deceased, who died before the publication of the notice referred to in sub section (1) of section 22B of the Income tax Act. The Income tax Officer found that on a correct interpretation of section 24B the amounts which were received by the heirs or legal representatives after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub sections (1), 2 and 3 of s.24B as his income in the hands of his heirs andlegal representatives but in the previous year and which had not been assessed but would have been assessed as income received by him if death had not taken place. The Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City held that on correct interpretation the amounts received by Amarchand after his demise should be treated as income for the purpose of assessment under section 24 B(1) (b) read with section 24A(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that on an incorrect interpretation of s 24B, the amounts were received subsequent to the previous years in which Amarchand died and therefore they were not liable to tax in the several years of assessment. Held: (i) The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section24B and cannot be extended further than the liability for the income received in the earlier year and are therefore not liable for tax in respect of those years. In the present case, the amount which were sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to income tax is those which were not received in that previous year but were income which may be deemed to have been received by his heirs or representatives after their death but in that case also the amount was earned by the deceased during the previous previous year.

Section 3 of the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957 provides that no citizen shall on ground only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State. Section 4(1)(a) empowers Parliament to make rules prescribing, in regard to appointments to (a)any subordinate service or post under the Government of Andhra Pradesh, or any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to such appointment. The first clause emphasises that ware shall be in India equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to an office under that State and, secondly, whether Par liament can delegate this function by making a declaration and leaving the details to be filled in by the rule making power of the Central or State Governments. The second clause emphasizes that ware will be in Indian equality of opportunities for all citizen in matters of employment or appointments to any office under, the late. For the original words of the clause 'under any State specified in the First Schedule or any local or other authority within its territory any requirement As to residence in parts of State such as Districts, talauqas, cities, towns etc. more appropriate and specific language could have been used such as 'any requirement as To residence within a State or any particular part of that state or Union Territory prior to the appointment, as a condition of employment in the State or the Union territory. Under article 35(a) this power is conferred upon Parliament but is denied to the Legislatures of the States notwithstanding anything in the Constitution, and under (b) any law in force immediately before the commencement of the Constitution in respect to the matter shall subject to the terms thereof and subject to such adaptations that may be made under article 372 is to continue in force until altered or repealed by Parliament. In view of our conclusion on this point it was not necessary to express any opinion whether delegation to the Central and/or State Governments to provide by rules for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament is valid or not.

The appellant, who was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them, also for offences punishable under sections 467 and 471 of the Penal Code. The Additional Sessions judge convicted the appellant and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives, the appellant cannot be said to have secreted the letter just because it was found in the almirah which is said to had been in his exclusive possession; (2) for an officer of the post office to be found guilty for any of the acts specified in section 52 it has further to be shown that he was entrusted with the postal article with respect to which he is alleged to have committed any of those acts. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The prosecution having failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the Appellant, they could not sustain an inference that the almirah was even in the appellant 's joint possession along with his father because he had the opportunity to get at the articles and then infer that he must have utilized the opportunity and was therefore in their exclusive possession would be theft but it has not been found that he had secreted them from the mere fact that they were found in his almirah which, at best, may be regarded as being in the joint possession of himself and his father. [413 D E] (b) The High Court could have held that though the locked almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the appellant could sustain an presumption that the envelope contained apart from the registered letter in question, certain other articles belonging either to the father and since he had an opportunity to procure the articles it could not be established by showing that he has secreted these articles.

The appellants were convicted of contempt of court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ and further ordered that in case of default they shall undergo simple imprisonment for two weeks. On December 20, 1963, Mahabir moved an application under article 227 of the Constitution challenging the order of the S.D.M., dated November 28, 1963 and on the same day the High Court admitted the application and stayed further proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Nyaya Panchas faithfully accepted the objections raised by the Sarpanch. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that there was no reasonable ground for the Panchas to have doubted the averments made in the application; and (2) that the High court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the S,D. M., had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of Court. Contempt of court is a serious matter and a High Court should be chary of finding a judicial Officer guilty of contempt for disobeying its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge of the order passed by the High Courts. [119 E F] (ii) The application did not contain the .date of the High 'Court 's stay order. It was no part of the duty of the Panchachas to enquire from the S and D.M. about the filing of the application before him. It could only be adjourned for enable the party to file fresh proof, and if it bona fide did not in its discretion adjourn proceeding it cannot he said that the order was passed deliberately to by pass the order.

The appellant was taken in custody and as a result of the investigation, he was sent up for trial. He denied the allegation that he had caused the death of Sheo Sahai and alleged that he was falsely accused of the offence. The Sessions Judge rejected his statement on the ground that it was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offences by the appellant made to a Police Officer and that the evidence about the purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant 's conviction and sentence were insufficient to establish conclusively that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai. On appeal, the High Court held that the entire report dictated by the accused was inadmissible as its Contents amounted to confession of an offence by the Appellant made to the Police Officer. The High Court also rejected the statement of Ujagar Singh about the recovery of a sword from his field on account of the crops being not very high and which made them doubt the appellant "s confessing to him that he did commit the murder of Sheo Saran or not, as it was not unlikely that the accused should have made a statement that he might have committed the murder. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that the High court erred in rejecting the statement Of Ujagar Singh regarding the recovery and the extra judicial confession together with the circumstances relied on by the High Courts, fully supported by Paley Singh, P.W. 2, who deposed about the sale of a weapon to the appellant on June 13, 1960; (ii) that even if the mere possession of a bottle so stained be not sufficient to establish positively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder had committed the offence, would be feeling so justified in his conduct as to openly admit it to the first person he met and to go to the police station and report about it; (iii) that there was evidence about it, which made it very likely that what he stated did happen, there could not have appeared any improbability in Ujagar Singh 's sleeping in his field and meeting the appellant in the manner alleged, particularly when the learned Judges believed, and there was no evidence about this. The evidence of P.Ws. 2 and 3 corroborated by the medical evidence showed that the deceased had been taken to the hospital at about mid night on June 14, 1960. It was further contended for him that the extrajudicial confession togetherwith the circumstances relating thereto were sufficient to prove conclusively that it must be the appellant who committed the crime of murder of a person with whom he had enmity, had committed his murder. Held: (1) The High court was wrong in rejecting this statement of Palei Singh regarding recovery and extra judicial confessions made by the appellants in their report dictated at the Police Station and considered the case against the appellant. It is no doubt unusual, as urged for the respondent, that a person who commits a murder in pursuance of an enmity arising out of minor disputes would be feel feeling so unjustified in his behaviour as to orally admit it To the first one he met; and (2) that a man who commits an offence in pursuance Of an enmity arose out of major disputes, would not be feeling So justified in the conduct as a to openly admitting it to his first person.

The appellants filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court praying for quashing the electoral roll and the calendar of events issued for the purpose of the said election and directing the respondents to refrain from conducting the poll on December 31, 1978 in all the 44 constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants herein presented a claim to include his name in the electoral rolls on October 19, 1978 and that was rejected by the Deputy Collector without following the procedure prescribed for the purposes. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days from the date of publication of that notice when sub rule (3) of Rule 4 of the rules prescribed that such claims and objection could be preferred and in paragraph 7 thereof it had been stated that any such claim or objection filed beyond the prescribed period was liable to be rejected. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners were entitled to the issue of the writ prayed for as of right and the delay in filing the petition should have been ignored. On the facts and in the circumstances of the case, it was only on December S, 1978 for the first time that the attention of the Collector was drawn to the said error and that the writ petition itself was presented on December 28, 1978. No satisfactory explanation was given in the course of the petition by the petitioners as to why they delayed the filing of the Petition till December 28. 1978 even though they knew that there was an error in the notices issued under sub rule(3) Of Rule 4 (1)of the Rules in the month of October, 1978 more than two months before the date on which i, was filed. It is not the case of the petitioners that they did not know immediately after the publication of such notice that in the said notice a period o 20 days had been mentioned in its preamble as the period within which the claims and/or objections could be made and in para 7 thereof, it has been stated by them that any claim or objections filed beyond that prescribed period were liable to rejection. It was notified that the nominations could be filed on and after November 25, 1978 but the poll, if necessary, would take place on December 30, 1978 even although they knew knowledge that there had been an error of the notice issuing under Rule4(1). No satisfactory explanations was given by the petitioner as to how they delayed filing of their petition till December 31.1978 even though he knew that it was an erroneous notice issued in the months of October 21, 1978 much than two days before the said date on whose i, were filed. The writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High court as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay and the writ Petition itself was rightly rejected by it as there is no satisfactory reason for the delayed filing thereof. [417C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the petitioners were not entitled to any issue of right or the delay on the ground that they had not known immediately after publication of the notification under Rule 3(1), nor did they know immediately thereafter before the publication. No proper explanation was furnished in the petition as to what prevented them from filing their claim and/ or objections thereto within a specified period. [404E F] 2:2 It is difficult to place any reliance on the above news item for the object of concluding that the Collector, Raipur had been informed about the defect of the notices issuing under sub Rule (3), of Rule 8 of the Act by October 21. 1978 more nearly two months after the date when i, is filed.

The 1st respondent company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The 1st appellant company and its directors filed a complaint against the 2nd respondent company for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the , which was punishable under sub section (3) of that section. The High Court held that if no balance sheet is laid before a general body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balancesheet and profit or loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of Companies Act 1913 or section 220 of the . In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the decision necessarily led to the conclusion that even in a prosecution under section 134 of the 1913 Act, the company and their directors could not rely upon their failure to call the general meeting as a defence to the prosecution; (ii) the fact that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meetings. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The principle laid down in Park vs Lawton(8) was applied and it was held that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section134 of the Companies Act or section 221 of the 1956 Act as the case may be, while wilful omission from calling a general Body meeting and omit to lay a balance sheet or profit and for not sending a statement of the fact of the reasons therefore have to be annexed to the balance sheets and to the copies thereof required to be filed with the registrar; (iii) section 134 lays down that after balance sheet, and profit & loss account or the income and expenditure account, as thecase may be have been laid before the company at general meeting three copies thereof shall be filed alongwith the Registrar. If no balancesheet is laid within a special body, it is obvious that no copies of the balance Sheet so laid before it can expose the persons responsible to punishments under other sections of the Income Tax Act or Section 220 of that Act as, the case might be, when wilful omission in calling a particular general body meeting and omitting to lay down the balance-sheet and profits before it could expose the company to punishment udder aforesaid provisions. [417 B C] (2) In the instant case, on principle and authority it should be held that none of the High Courts which have considered this question after the decision of this Court had proceeded on the basis that the decision must necessarily lead to the inference that even if no general body meet is held, it was obvious that copies of such documents so laid should be filed before the Registrar but nonetheless if the requirements are not complied with even then, the persons concerned would be liable for punishment for that default. Under section 134, the laying of a balancesheet or profit account before an annual general meeting is a condition precedent to the requirement that copy of such document so laid must be filed at the general meetings three copies whereof shall be sent under sub sections (1), (2), (3), (4) and (5) of Section 134. But section 135 lays down, that after Balance sheet and profits and expenditure accounts before an Annual general meeting are made obligatory, a statement by that fact and of reasons therefore has to be attached to the Balance Sheet and profit, which is laid at a general Meeting.

Section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act lays down that "a special court shall try such offences or classes of cases as, in its opinion, require speedier trial". Section 5(2) empowers the State Government to direct any case to be tried by a Special Court according to the special procedure provided by it for the speediers trial of certain offences. The appellant contended that section 5 (1) was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution in so far as it purported to vest in the State government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, "whether the duration of such a case is likely to be long or not ". Held, that section 4 (1)(a) of West Bengal special Courts Act laid down that offences triable by the Special Court shall try those offences and classes of offences or class of cases, as the State Govern ment may, by general or special order in writing direct". The object being, as a matter of construction, that the preamble is to be read as a part of section 5(l), it follows that the object by itself cannot be the basis of the classification of offences and the cases, for, in the absence of any special circumstances which may dis tinguish one offence or one class of offences from another offence, or class or of offences, speedien trial is desirable in the disposal of all offences or Classes of cases. The difference between cases and offences triable under the Special Courts and those by ordinary courts is indicated in the preamble to the Act which runs as follows: "Whereas it is expedient to provide for the speedy trial of such offences and to make provision for speedi er trial of those offences; It is, therefore, necessary to ascertain whether it is actually based on a reasonable classification of the persons to whom or the offences in respect of which the procedure laid down in it is to apply, and if any charge of discrimination can be levelled at all, it can be leveled only against the act of the executive authority if the Act is misused.

The appellant, who was a Radiologist in the Maulana Azad Medical College and treated as an Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in Maulana Safdarjang Hospital, New Delhi, filed a writ petition before the High Court contending that he possessed the essential educational qualification and had also the requisite teaching experience while holding the post of Radiologist cum Associate Professor in the concerned speciality as required under the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there is a distinction between the two posts of Radiological and Associate Professors of Radiology as the post which the appellant holds in the Irwin Hospital is akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate professor in the Willing don Hospital or the Safdarjung Hospital and the mere designation of the appel lant as such does not give him a right to hold the post. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The designation of an appellant as a Radiographer cum Associate professor of Radiography (ex officio) by the University of Delhi does not make him eligible for appointment to the post as Professor of radiotherapy under r. (2) of the Central Civil Health Service Rules, 1963, particularly when the Central Government have been utilizing his services as such for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students of the Maurulana Azad medical College for the M.D., M.S., D.M.R.T. and MB.B.S. courses of studies for the last 17 years. The appellant who was holding a non clinical post in a teaching hospital like the IrSHwin Hospital, has been actually teaching the students of Maulana Ansari Medical College to which it is affiliated. [8H; 8A] 2. There is some difference between the posts of radiologist and Associate Professor as the Post of Radiographer is a teaching post. That being so, it was urged that the designation of appellant as such did not give his right to holding the office of Associate Professor or Radiology in Ma ul Azad Medical college. By parity of reasoning, it is urged that he has not acquired the status of an Associate professor or Radiologist with effect from October 9, 1964, particularly since the Central Govern ment have been utilising his services for teaching of the post Graduate and undergraduate students of M.M., D.,M.S, D. M.R.,T. & M.B., B.D.M, R.K. Medical College.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in this appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. The first and the main point argued was that there were other industries in the region in which minimum wages were higher than the minimum wage paid by the Company, but failed to fix the minimum wages in the award in accordance with the minimum rates being paid in those industries. Held, that the Tribunal committed no error of law requiring interference by this Court, in basing its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of 1959 and in holding that there was no justification to introduce a new element of payment of bonus to casual and badIi workers at this stage. The claim was based on the circumstances that according to the workmen, the bonus in their case was being calculated as equivalent to three months ' basic wages, while, the case of some clerical staff, the calculation was made on the basis of their consolidated wages consisting of basic wages and dearness allowance. In such cases, the principle which is being applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rate of three months' basic wage in each case and in no case is the dearness allowance taken into account. The Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and, at the time of reference at least, there was not and there could possibly be a claim for higher bonus on the ground that, under the agreement of 1959, the workmen and the Company had agreed specifically to exclude these classes of workers in regard to payment of Bonus.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. The Income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. He observed that "in fact this income arose from a statutory obligation of the Government to pay it, and although the Government recouped this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appears in the second degree, its immediate and effective source is the Government 's statutory obligation to pay the same, and that is so notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the income, a substantial part whereof is derived from lands used for agricultural purposes." The Appellate Tribunal held that the right which was conferred by section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act, 1922, was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that according to the true interpretation of the letter dated July 7, 1837, Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors were granted in perpetuity a right of one third of the land revenue collection itself and not merely a right in the land or in land revenue, but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The source of the pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the respondent was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4 (3)(vii) of Income tax. [757 B] (2) The income of a trust appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration is not received by him as rent or revenue of land; the character of the property appropriated as remuneration due is again not the same as the character in which it was received by the assessee as trustee. Both the source and character of income are, therefore, altered when a part of the net income of trust is appropriated by an appellant as His remuneration, and this obligation is not land within the ambit of the definition in section 2(1)(a) of Indian Income tax, 1922. [758 C D] (3) It follows from the decisions of the Privy Council and the judgments of this Court cited above that if it is held in this case that the source of a allowance or pension is the arrangement arrived at in 1837. then the income cannot be held to be derived from land within, the meaning Of the definition In section 2 (1)(b) of The Indian Income Tax Act, 1961.

Section 47(1 H) prescribes that in the case of inter State route, the Undertaking will have preference in the matter of stage carriage permit. Clause (iv) of the proviso to section 63(7) provides that where in pursuance of an approved scheme a State Transport Undertaking applies for a stage carriage permits, a contract carriage permit or a public carrier 's permit in respect of a notified area or notified route shall be granted to the State Transport Authority in a case where the said area or route lies in more than one region and the Regional Transport Authority is satisfied that the State transport Undertaking would be able to operate in the inter State routes without detriment to its responsibility for providing efficient and adequate road transport services in any notified area, or notified notified route. Section 68 F(1) provides for preference to be given to applications for permits from the Indian Tourism Development Corporation, the State Tourist Department and the State tourist Department were not questioned, but the preference provided for by clause (iv), was questioned as an infringement of article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The word 'preference ' occurring in section 47( 1 H) does not say for example, like section 68 F that the permit has to be necessarily granted to a State transport undertaking. [1015C D] The general scheme of the Act in the matters of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the cases of a specified notified route or notified area the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. Section 19(1) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 empowers the State Government to make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act, but the section cannot be utilised to enlarge the scope of section 10 regarding recovery and payment of tax from some other person other than a "dealer" under the Act. The word "assessment" used in section 19(2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other then the transferee of the business is constituted as the dealer liable to pay the tax in respect of his turnover and under the scheme of the charging provision of the State Act, the purchaser of the property has nothing to do with the sales effected by the seller of the said business. Held, that Rule 21 A is beyond the rule making power of the state Government either under section 19 (1) or section 19 of the Kerala General Sales tax (3rd amendment) Act, 1956 and as it was published in the Madras Gazette on October 8, 1956, the Act came into operation on that date and not before. [922 B] (ii) Where, immediately before the appointed day, the State of Bombay has made any contract in the exercise of its executive power for any purposes of the State, that liability shall, if the cause of action arose wholly within the territories which, as from that day, are the territories of the States of Maharashtra and Gujarat or, in default of such agreement, as the Central Government may by order direct. The liability arising under the declaration that the appellant was in Government service is the liability of the state within the ambit of section 62 of the Indian . [923 C D].

The appellant was the lessee of a coal mine. On August 18, 1941, the plaintiffs made an inquiry and came to know that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. The respondents ' predecessor in interest stated that they were aware that the portion of coal land in question belonged to and was the property of the appellant, and that Seam Nos. But to say that no duty is cast upon the plaintiff even to allege the date when they had knowledge of the defendant 's possession of the converted property and that the entire burden is on the respondents to prove that they had known the sinking of the quarries and pits in the encroached land. Held, further, that under the Indian Mines Act and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder the defendants could request the mining authorities to exempt them from the operation of rule 76 of the Indian Coal Mines Regulation, 1946, and if exemption was granted, they could remove the coal left by the appellant in the encroachment area. In other words, he has to prove, that he obtained the knowledge of a defendant ' s possession of his property within three years of the date of the filing of the suit, and, therefore, the coal that is still left in the encroach area was lost to them by being rendered unworkable. Held further, also, that the burden of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondents beyond the prescribed time was on the appellant as it had given the finding on the assumption that the initial burden was on them.

The appellant was a crosscutter carrying on business in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. On June 21, 1958 Sankaran was informed that in view of his denial, a departmental inquiry would be held and he was also placed under suspension pending inquiry. On July 8, 1958, the appellant terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18 (a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran the same day. In the meantime Sankaran was intimated that in spite of his refusal, a Departmental Enquiry would be conducted and he had been placed under suspended pending inquiry and disciplinary proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r, 18(a) and (b) of Standing Orders. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Held: (i) There is nothing more to be said and that the industrial court cannot inquire into the causes that led to the termination of service under a rule like 18(A) and if it is satisfied that the action taken under such a rule was a colourable exercise of power and was not bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. (ii) The employer could defend the action under r., 18(b) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action took under r . 18(c) was bona fide and was therefore not colourable exercise Of the power conferred.

The appellants filed a suit in the Court of Small Causes at Ahmedabad against Raval and Faraqui and two other persons claiming a declaration that it 437 was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The Trial Judge held that the consent decree had not decided that the transaction between the parties of the year 1954 was in the nature of a lease; that in view of the said consent decree the defendants 5 and 6 were estopped from contending and leading any evidence and putting questions in cross examination of plaintiffs witnesses to show that the said document dated November 27, 1954 as confirmed by their letter dated January 31, 1955 and further confirmed by document dated December 01, 1960 was not a lease. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the suit No. 149 of 1960 was for declaration of the rights of Filmistan to exhibit Motion pictures in theatre under the agreement on the ground that it related to a matter to be decided by the Court and on which the opinion of witnesses was irrelevant; that the question whether in fact the subordinate Court had decided the question of res judicata, and that in the plaint in the earlier suit it was not even averred that the rights granted were in the character of leasehold rights; that as the question was already concluded by the consent judgment decree in suit No 149 of 1961, the defendants Nos. 5 and 7 were estopped therefrom from contending or leading any further evidence and put questions in crossexamination of plaintiffs witness to show their terms and language; and that the agreement of December 1 1960 was "not plain enough to exclude the oral evidence of the surrounding circumstances and conduct of the parties to explain its terms and words". Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1) The question whether the legal relationship arising out of the agreement between December 1. 1960 and November 27 1954 was a lease or of other character had to be determined at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent, "could not operate as res judicata" for, it was never decided in Major section Khanna 's case that every order of the Court in the course of a suit amounts to a case decided within the meaning of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The only thing that can be said is that so far as the agreement in question is con cerned, it must be held, in view Of the consent terms decree of December 27,1954, that that document of November 27. 1954 created a lease and that there after the High Court could, if the matter were brought before it by way of appeal or in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, have decided that question and allow the whole question, that was closed once for all by consent decree 'could be reopened, it is proposing to exercise the jurisdiction which is not vested in it by law. Once the jurisdiction of the court has been taken away, any proposal to reopen the question closed by the earlier decision would be exercise of jurisdiction which was not vested with the Court by law and to that extent the decision would become revisable even if it is the decision as to the res judicata of an issue." (2) The order passed by the High court is set aside and the Trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit.

The respondent, Arun Govil was granted a permanent commission in the Indian Air Force and was working as a Pilot Officer. In the year 1972 he was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The term of the respondent had come to an end on 30th August, 1985 as stated above and no further order of extention had been passed by the Governor. The respondent aggrieved by the said order filed a Writ Petition before the High Court contending that he was enti tled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period of his appointment beyond 30th of August,1985. The High Court allowed the Review Petition and made an order reinstating the Respondent in service which reads as follows: "This is an application for review of our Judgment dated 24.3.1988 by which we allowed the Writ Petition filed by the Petitioner with certain directions. It is not disputed that no order of 'extension had been sanctioned by the Government beyond 30.8.1985. Since it was admitted that no orders of extension had been granted by the Gover nor of Uttar Pradesh, the respondent was entitled to salary and allowances due to him till 30th July, 1985 if the order of termination of service served on him on 29.3..1988 was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment upto 30th September, 1985 were liable to be ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years." The High court allowed the writ petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ Petitions were liable ted. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the High court had while setting aside the order dated 24th March, 1988 directed that the respondent should be reinstated into service irrespective Of the merits of the case and the extent of his right. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The scheme under which the respond ent was appointed provided for an appointment by contract for a specified term which could be extended from time to time and that the term of office had come into an end after his first appointment and he was not entitled to continue in service beyond 30 days of August 1985 unless there was a further extension. [243E] 2. The appointment of the responde ent was indisputably in the character of contract and under the last order of appointment refened to above he was entitled for salary and allowance due to them till he complete the age Of 58 years. His only case was that the interim order that had been made on 10.7.86 entitled him to be reinstate in service even though his service had not been extended by the Govern ment nor of U.P. or Uttar Pradesh. 1988 declaring that the Respondent was entitled, to salary upto the period he was entitle to remain in service, i.e., 30th day of August. 1985. [244E F] 3. The interim order did not and could not amount to a direction that the respondents were entitled to be reinstatement in service regardless of the merits o f the case. If the respond ed was really aggrieved by his judgment he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that was not right in making an order on Review on 26.7,1988 relying upon the Interim order dated 10.07.1986 which in the circumstances could not have the effect of controlling the jurisdiction of the High Courts to dispose of the Writ petition on merits as it did on 24.03.1988. [245G H] 4.

The appellant was acquitted by the Additional Sessions judge, Chittoor of an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court reversed the acquittal on the ground that there were two divergent versions given by the prosecution and the defence and when two views were possible, the benefit of doubt should be given to the accused. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) An injury of the nature received by the deceased could not have been caused in the manner suggested by the defence that it was, when the deceased was lying on her right side. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. If the evidence is so strong against a man as to leave only a remote possibility in his favour, which can be dismissed with the sentence 'of course it is possible but not in the least probable ' the case is proved beyond reasonable doubt, but nothing short of that will suffice. [368C D] (2) An accused person may claim, must be reasonable even as any doubt, the benefits of which an accused person might claim, should be reasonable. If he has been upset with fanciful doubts, rejects creditworthy evidence for slender reasons and takes a view of the evidence which is but barely possible, it is the obvious duty of the High Court to interfere in the interest of justice, lest the administration of justice be brought to ridicule. [369B C] (3) An order of acquittal is reversed by the High court merely because another view is also possible. If an accused is entitled to the benefit Of a doubt arising from the possibility of a duality of views, the possible view in favour of the accused must be as nearly reasonably probable as that against him.

Section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 provides that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under Section 5 of this Act alleged to have been committed by a public servant i.e. the Judge of the High Court includ ing the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court as in the present case, except with the previous sanction under clause (c) in the case of any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his office. The power to punish a High Court Judge if one may so describe it is to be found only in article 2 18 read with Article 124(4) and (5) of that Constitution for removal of the Judge as in section 5(1) of Prevention of corruption Act,1947. But that is not the position in the cases of removal of a Judge. The difficulty of sanction under Section 6 for the prosecution of superior Judges and the special provisions contained in clauses (4)and (5), of Article 124 read with article 124(5) is a clear pointer in the direction that the Parliament has not as yet considered it expedient to enact any such law for the trial and punishment on the charge of corruption of a superior Judge, except by his removal from office in the manner provided in Article 124, clauses 4 and 5 of the Constitution for removing the Judge from his Office. The incumbent of the office of Chief Justice exercises only moral authority over his colleagues in the Supreme court and the High Courts, which has no legal sanction behind it making it justiciable. It is for this reason that the learned Solicitor General did not place reliance on clauses (a) and(b) of Sub section (1) Of Section 6 in the instant case but relied on clause (d) thereof to contend that sanction thereunder can be obtained for prosecution of a person holding such an office. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Chief Justice exercising only moral power over his subordinates in the High court and Supreme Court Judges cannot be treated as the competent authority to grant sanction in accordance with Section 6 of the Act in re spect of the offences provided in section 6 of Prevention Corruption Act 1947. [216C D] 2. It appears that Parliament did not enact any other law even then for the investigation into allegations of corruption against a superior judge and for his trial and punishments for that offence and rest content merely with enacting the , to provide for the procedure for remov al of a judge under Article 124 (4). [216D E] 3. The obligation of the Chief Judge exercising only administrative control over his subordinate colleagues in Supreme Court and High Courts is clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office, there being no such vertical hierarchy and the ChiefJustice of India having no legal authority behind it makes it justiciable.[216E F] 4. Section 6(i)(c), as the only punishment; and a special law enacted by the Parliament under Article124(5), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a inferior Judge instead of the general law was clearly visualized when the allegation is connected With his office in that manner, there is no such horizontal hierarchy and, the Chief Justices of India, which have no legal sanctions behind it make it justiciable; and this can be done only if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. Any provision which cannot apply to the Judges of the Apex Court, or for that matter even to the High Cour t Judges, since the Chief justice of India is not a vertical superior of any of them, there having been no such exceptional situation and the Special provisions contained therein cannot obviously apply to those Judges who have no power of superintendence even over the High courts.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste and not a member belonging to the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40. In the election petition, the respondent had stated that the appellant belonged to an independent caste which had nothing to do with Sunri caste and that it was, therefore, not open to him at the trial to contend as he appeared to have done. The Election Tribunal held that the Sahas were originally a smaller caste group within the Sunri Caste group of Sunirs known as Sahas. On appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD: (1) A person belonging to a Scheduled Caste or a Scheduled Tribe cannot claim, by virtue of his origin, to belong to the category specified in items 40 and 41 of the Schedule Castes specified in Item 40 for he said "these Saha families, within the fold of Sunri tribe". The word 'Saha ' in the expression 'excluding Sahas ' in item 39 must, without more. also refer to a caste group consisting of those Sunris who formed the larger caste group of Sahas, but not those within that caste who formed a smaller Caste group called Sahas or were only distinguished from the other Sunris by their surname, whatever might be their other characteristics" and have come to form a class apart from the rest of the Suniti caste. [391 D E] (2) The Tribunal was right in holding that the respondent 's case fell within item 40 because it rejected a contention advanced on behalf of the appellant that item 40 excluded Sahas from Sunirs by way of abundant caution, so that theSahas who had originally belonged to the group did not claim, By virtue of their origin,to belong to that caste but bore the surname Saha. The result then is that the Tribunal held the respondent to be a Sunri and a person belonging lo the Scheduled Castes specified therein was excluded from the Scheduled caste specified initem 40 for the appellant 's said " these Sahas families, distinguished themselves by their Surname, whichever might be its other characteristics".

The appellant was the tenant of a flat occupied by him in the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the complainant Mulchand Kodumal Bhatia, who was also to act as caretaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view that he entered into negotiations with the complain ant. The defence of the appel lant was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who had been also to work as caRetaker of the Flat anal, that the sum of money was not pugree but represented capital for 0 12 share in the business and as the com plainant was also required to be a caretakers of the flats, the sum Of Rs. 2,500 was paid back and received by him as a security against disposal, damage of furniture and it had been agreed that he would give him Rs. 30,000 to be given back on his return to the India.
