The Industrial Tribunal rejected the claim of the appellant holding that there was no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in the basic pay of individual workmen. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Industrial Tribunal and remanded the matter to the Industrial tribunal for a fresh decision on merits. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that the expression "flat increase" occurring in section 2(k)(i) of the , is wide enough to include all categories including Draughtsmen, and (2) that even if there was any change in the structure of the scales, there could be no justification for amending the award. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "Flat increase " occurring in Section 2(h)(i), is wide and comprehensive enough to cover all categories of Draughtsmen and Rs. 150/ per month was added to the pay of every other workman, who belonged to the Union staff, the financial load would increase to Rs.150/ in the case of other categories to the initial pay in the wage scales pertaining to those categories. [176B C] 2. The Tribunal had only revised the wage structure by increasing the salary on entry into the service and res 184 tructuring the scale of pay and never granted any adhoc increase of salary to all employees. It was clearly so intended by the Tribunal as is evident from the reference to "fillat increase of Rs. 100/ in The case of draftsmen and other workmen respectively, the revised wage scales had necessarily to commence with figures Rs. 200/ and Rs 100/ above the existing pay scales. Immediately after the award was pronounced, while the iron was still hot as it were, the employees apparently realised that the employer might take advantage of the circumstance that it was not clearly mentioned in the award that all the employees were to get additional pay of Rs 150/ and also might contend that the Tribunal had merely revised the pay scales by increasing its salary on Entry into the Service and res 185 tructaling the scale. Immediately thereafter the iron is still hot, as it was, the employee apparently realised, that the employers might take benefit of the situation that it is not clearly specified in the order that all employees were getting additional pay. The omission of the words to each employee first after the figure Rs. 160/ and again after the figures Rs 150/- and again thereafter after the word figure Rs 100/- and subsequently after the words figure Rs 10,000/ respectively had been added to pay of each Draughtsman and a sum of Rs 50,000 was added in the pay scale of Rs 200/ was added. [177E F] 3. The amendment order required the Tribunal to revise the scales of pay, and there was nothing in the body of the award to form the foundation on which the actual figures in the restructured pay scales can be made to rest. It cannot be the case that the figure of Rs, 150/ or Rs.100 was intended to each of the employees in the category of Draughtsman, and Rs, 100/ was add to the Pay of every others, who belongs to the union staff, and thus fell within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal.

Section 2(vi) (a) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 provides that any remuneration payable under any award or settlement between the employer and his employees shall be included in the main definition under section 2(vii). The appellant paid its employees only As. / 10 / per day and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the authority that section 15 was applicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages before the said definition was amended in 1958. Held, that section 2 (vi) as it stood at the relevant time, provides, inter alia, that wages means all remuneration capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would, if the terms of the ,contract of employment, express or implied, were fulfilled, be payable. It is true that under the unamended definition of Wages, rates of remuneration prescribed by an award could not be included. But it must be shown that they constitute part of the terms Of the contract of employment either express or explicit. If it is shown to the satisfaction of Industrial adjudication that the terms prescribed by the said award did amount to a contract ofemployment, the wage structure prescribed by that award cannot fall within section 2.(vi) of Act before it was amended. R. Chacko (1), where it has been observed by this Court that the very purpose for which industrial adjudication had been given the peculiar authority and right of making new contracts between employers and workmen makes it reasonable to think that even though the period of operation of the award and the period for which it remained binding on the parties may elapse in respect of both of which special provisions have been made under sections 23 and 29 respectively the new contract would continue to govern the relations between the parties till it is replaced by another contract. The very purpose of making industrial adjudication, during the last decade bears testimony to the fact that on references made under section 10(1) of The Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1958 terms of employment have constantly been examined by industrial adjudication and wherever it appeared appropriate to make changes in them, they have been making in accordance with the well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed certain works at a place called Karhali. The trial Magistrate held that proof that the thumb impression in the acquittance roll was that of the appellant was sufficient to establish an offence either under section 465 or section 409 Of the Indian penal Code and that there having been an acquittal of the accused by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section409 Of the Government of India Act, 1935 and that the evidence on record was insufficient to establish the offence either by virtue of his office or that there had been an acquitted of the charge by the trail Magistrate. HELD: (i) The prosecution which has resulted in the conviction of the Appellant was initiated without any sanction under s 197(I) of Code of criminal Procedure and if sanction under that section is necessary, as contended for by Mr. According to the respondent, however, the main charge against the appellant is under section misappropriation, and no sanction is required for a prosecution under that Section. [1305 B C] (ii) It was not every offence committed by a public servant that requires sanction for prosecution under section 196(1), of the Criminal Procedure Code; nor even every act done by him while he is actually engaged in the performance of his official duties; but if the act complained of is directly concerned with his official duty so that, if questioned, it could be claimed to have been done by virtue Of the office, then sanction would be necessary; and that would be so irrespective of whether it was, in fact a proper discharge of his duties, because that would really be a matter of defence on the merits which would have to be in vestigated at the trial, and could not arise at the stage of the grant of sanction, which mu_t precede the institution of the prosecution. But he contends that misappropriation of funds could, under no circumstances, be said to be within the scope of his duty, that he could not, when charged with it, claim justification for it by virtue o his office, that therefore no sanction under Section 197(l) was necessary and that in view of the decisions in Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor (1) and Albert We8 Meads vs The King (2), in both of which the charges were of criminal misappropriation, the material on record could not justify any reversal of the verdict by this Court.

The assessee, a resident of the erstwhile State of Cochin, was carrying on business in British India and was assessed to income tax under section 12B of the Travancore Income tax Act of Travancore. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee: (i) that business losses were incurred in British Indian States only to business or to modify the mode of computation under section 10 of the Indian Act; (ii) that the first proviso to section 24(1) of the Act not only affected the generality of the main enactment but also introduced an addendum that where the profits of the business arose in what was British India in the case of the Cochin Act and the losses under the head business were sustained in an Indian state or in the latter case in any other Indian State or British India, these losses could not by virtue of the proviso be deducted from profits made during British India or Travancore State as the case may be. HELD: (1) The mere use of the words loss of profits or gains to be, set off under section 9(2)(c) does not justify the construction. that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising under the heads business in the two territories, i. e., British India & the Indian States. (ii). The mere fact that the word " income" is not used does not lead to an interpretation which would support an interpretation in favour of the disintegration of the head " business" and chargeability of total income under section 3 or the provisions Of section 4 where in the cases of a resident "total income" includes income, profits and gains accruing within or without British India is to ignore the definitions and sections 3, 4 and 6. But then it was said that as the profits or losses arising in Indian States were exempted from payment of tax in British country business in section 10 must mean business in India or business the profits and gain accruing within, or without I British India are to ignore, the definition and sections 2, 4, 5 and 6 must be read together. (iii)The mere use by the words " loss of profit or gains" to be setoff against profits and profits would not be sufficient to restrict that scope of the provisos to the profitsand losses arising from Indian States merely to business, profession or vocation to modify mode of calculation under section10 of theIndian Act. The mere existence of the word ' income ' does not support an construction in favour Of the disastration of head "business" and Chargeability of Total income under Section 3 or of the provisions o. 4 where the loss sustained is a loss of business or vocation, to which the first Proviso to sub section (1), is applicable. But it was urged on behalf for the Revenue that the words ' loss of income ' are not used did not justify this construction. The intention of Parliament was to confine the setoff of profits under one head against income, profit or gain arising within British India only to trade or to alter the mode or computation under Section 10 of Indian Act. But in the proviso in dispute there were no positive words which would enable an interpretation to be given to the main section and compel the application of the said proviso to the same heads, specially keeping in view the object of the sub section, i.,e., section 24 (1).

The respondent company was governed by the West Bengal Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. The workmen claimed that these showed clearly a tendency in comparable concerns in Bombay region to fix the retirement age at 60 years, that is, between 1952 and 1961; that in recent years at least the tendency in similar concerns in Calcutta region had been to fix retirement age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60; that the trend in Bombay has been to fixing the retirement ages at 60. On a consideration of all the facts and circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on this record, it was found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Madras region the trend had beento fix the retire ment age at 58 subject to certain employees passing the medical examination; that there is no indication at all as to how long ago the age was fixed at 60 and not at 55; and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal, was in fact inaccurate. On the question of age of superannuation it was contended on behalf of the workmen that (1) the trend of Bombay region had not been to fixed the retirement Age of retirement at 60, (2) the Tribunal had found that there was a general agree ment that the age should be fixed at 58; and (3) its present conclusions that what were said by themselves on an later occasion and were confirmed by the Supreme Court in appeals. Held: (i) The Tribunal 's finding that in some of the awards there is a general agreement with regard to the relevant trend must be strong and unambiguous and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter, was on the whole unsound. On an examination of all these facts it was clear that the Tribunal has failed to notice that instances which may justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an previously occasion about a particular trend must always be strong, and unambiguous, they must speaks for the periods both before, and more especially after the earlier finding had already been recorded. The very few departures from this practice which the Tribunal have mentioned are, in our opinion, wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. What is said by a Committee on which both employers and employees were represented emphasised the fact that in the Bombay region at least there was general agreeion that the. age of retire should be fix at 60 but on a consideration Of all the relevant material and relevant circumstances, and that one of the important material considerations in this connection would be whether the conclusion recorded by the Tribunal in some other cases as to the particular trend in the Mumbai region was correct.

The appellants were convicted on the sole evidence of having in their possession pieces of cloth which were later identified to belong to the traders. They were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced them to ' 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,000/ . The High Court and the Court below drew from this the conclusion that the appellants were themselves the dacoits and convicted them accordingly under section 412 of the I.P.C., but not of complicity in the crime of dacoity and therefore as they could be suspected to be dacoits themselves, the only presumption to be drawn ought to have been one under section 41 1 722 of Indian Penal code or at the most tinder section 412 Of the Indian. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on their behalf that the circumstances under which the one presumption or the other may be drawn under section 114 of the had not been stated by law and therefore it was necessary always to start with the lesser presumption only when there is some other evidence to show the complicity of the persons in the offence itself. Held, that a sentence of three years ' imprisonment will meet the ends of justice in this case. The presumption is stronger when the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is. committed. Disposal of the fruit of crime requires the finding of a person ready to receive them and the shortness of time, the nature of the property which is disposed of, that is to say, its quantity and its character determine whether the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thief or the dacoit. In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be draw. They need not be stated here for they differ from case to case.(In the present case, the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen.) A large number of persons said to be the dacoits themselves. It may be 723 that if the gap of time is, too short, the presumption that the accused was concerned with the crime itself, however small, the finding that the person was concernedwith the crime himself, is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence.

The assessee firm applied to the Tribunal under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 to refer the following question to the High Court of Madras "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off as irrecoverable in the books of account was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the assessee ?" HELD : (i) The debt in question was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending businesses nor a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. It contains only a summary of the business relations between the appellants and the Bombay firm, a statement as to the amounts due at the end of each year at the foot of the account, the interest if any charged and a summary thereof. The failure to adjust interest in the account of the Bombayfirm at the stage at which it became a debtor in Samvat Year 2007, the manner in which the partner of the appellant firm tried to explain the position in March, 1954 and the stand of the firm itself at all earlier stages support the case of the Department. [12 D E] (ii) The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the assessee to the Bombay Firm were not loans made in the ordinary course of the money lending trade of the appellants nor in respect of any other business of it, nor in regard to any other income of the assesses. In view of this finding, which is binding on this Court, our answer to the question reframed has to be in the negative and in favour of the Revenue.

The land of the extent of four acres was carved out and given to the Taj Group of Hotels for the construction of a Five Star Hotel. The land allotted to the hotel was, as we have seen, not used for the main purpose of the zoo for the purpose of construction of five Star hotels. It was not forgotten that if the land was to be allotted to it, separate provision would have to be made for whatever use the land is being put to them. The Government of West Bengal appeared to have been on the search for two suitable plots of land which could be offered, one to the I.T.D.C. and the other to the Zoo logical Garden upon the terms set out in the two letters. In the face of all this material, it is clear that the Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of the Zoological Garden upon a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Govern ment in taking a particular action, that the Court would have had to decide whether the action of the Government is reasonable and in public interest. But in a case like this where the State is allo cating resources such as water, power raw materials etc. for the purposes of encouraging setting up of industries within the State, we do not think the State was bound to advertise and tell the people that it wants a particular industry to be set up within the state and invite those interested to come up with pro posals for thepurpose. On a consideration of all the facts and circumstances brought out by the appellants do not justify an inference that the construction in the Begumbari land would interfere in any manner with the animals in the Zira and the birds arriving at the ZOO or otherwise disturb the ecology: The proposed hotel is a Garden hotel and there is perhaps every chance of the ecology and environment improving as a result of planting numerous trees all around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and dumping ground for rubbish. It is on a total consideration of various factors which have weigh with the Government in taking an particular action that the court would have required to decide, whether the act of the Govt is reasonable or in public interests. But, in a ease like this, where the state has made available to this Court all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of the State Government land to respondent No. 1, the Chief Minister 's assurances are found reflected in the lease executed by the Taj group of Hotels in favour of the Governm ent and it is on such a total appraisal of various consideration which have been weighed with th e Government in formulating its policies and it was on atotal evaluation of several considerations which had weighed with tapping contract simpliciter, that this calculation conveniently forgets that what is involved here is not the sale of the land but a lease by the Government, as a policy decision to the Hotel group to start a Five star hotel. Bearing in mind the proper approach that we have to make when 263 questions of ecology and environmental environment are raised, an approach which we have mentioned at the outset, we are satisfied that the facts brought out in by the appel lant do not warrant an inference of any resin being sold in the open market. The matter was taken in appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Government acted perfectly bona fide in granting the lease of Begumbar land to the zoological Park for the construc tion of a five Star hotel in Calcutta.

The assessee was assessed to wealth tax under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957. The Income Tax Officer held that the assessee did not make valid gifts aggregating Rs. 1,50,000 on 1.1.1957 and that the sum of Rs.67,560/ was rightly included in the net wealth of the assessee. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court held that there was no valid gift on the date of entries, then it could not be held that, subsequently, when the money was transferred by further entries in the same books, it resulted in a valid gift. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (1) In case there was not sufficient cash balance from out of which the amount gifted could be physically given to the donee, more entries in his account in the form would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the donor and gift in such case will not be valid. [129E] (2) The assessee had made a valid gifts of the value of Rs 1 lakh and Rs.50,00,000 to his wife, K, by making debit entries in their accounts in the firm and corresponding credits to the accounts of L and K. The gift was held to be valid under section 10 of the Act. [130F] (3) In the case of Virji Devshi vs Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P., , the Bombay High Court had occasion to refer to the effect of book entries but this question which is present before this Court in that case was not before this court in that particular case. The Allahabad High Court has also taken divergent views. On a question arising whether there was a valid Gift or trust in respect of the said amounts, it was held by the Division Bench of the Madras High Court that there had been no completed gift of the principal amount as there was nothing on record to show that the interests which were credited in the account of the minor donees by the firm which carried on money lending business also were fictitious. [131F G] (4) In cases where there is not sufficient money balance from outside out of the books of account, then a valid transfer by book entries might be possible but where a sum was not available with the firm or the family or a company which was not a banking company or which had no overdraft facility, by mere book entry even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would not effectuate a valid marriage.

Section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Preemption Act, 1913 provides that where the sale is by a female of land or property to which she has succeeded through her husband, or through her son in case the son has inherited the land orproperty sold from his lather, the right of pre emption shall vest First, in the sons or daughters or son 's son or daughter 's sons of the vendor or vendors; Thirdly, in a father 's brother or mother 's brothers or brother 's sister 's father ' or vendors Fifthly n the tenants, who hold under tenancy of the vendors or any one of them the land, or property sold or a part thereof. (iii) if the sale was by the son ordaughter of such female, in case of a co sharer and has not been made by all the co sharers jointly, only the other co shar ties and the tenants can exercise the right conferred on them by that provision. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The legislature desired to confer the right to pre emention on specified family members of the vendee or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section 15(i)(b) and with a view to covering all the remaining co shars not specifically mentioned the preceding clauses it used the expression 'other co sharERS ' in the fourth clause which was meant to serve as a residuary clause to ensure 127 that, no co shar er is left out. [127A B] 1.2 The legislature wanted to confer a right of preemption on certain specified family member of the seller or vendors in the first three sub clauses of Section 15(I)(b). This Court, therefore, did not find any justification for the classification contained in section 15 which conferred a right on the kinsfolk. [128E F] 1:3 In the instant case also this Court held that the purport of the of Court 's decision in Attam Prakash 's case was to deny the right under pre emtion to those relative or relatives of the purchaser or vendors, who were not specified in sub clauses (1) and (c) even if they happen to be co shar ers. [129E F; 128A] 1 :4 In the context, it becomes clear that the legislature desired that confer the rights of pre Emption on specified Family members of a vendor or vendor in the second three clauses. This Court did not found any justification either for the classify contained in Section 15 which imposed a right to hold acquire or dispose of property conferred by Article 19(1) (f) and clause fourthly of section15(1). [128F G] 1.:5 In Attam Parkash vs State of Haryana & Ors., ; , followed.

Allowing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The compromise petition shall be accepted and in terms thereof the suit shall be disposed of and the terms of the compromise shall form part of the order to be drawn up in this Court for disposing of the special Leave Petition. [540D E] 2.1 In view of the fact that there had been the allegation of payment of Rs. 1 lakh to Sudarshan Gupta which we have not investigated and to meet the further allegation that some improvements have been made to the property which too we have no gone into, the Court is directed by our present order to deliver vacant possession of the entire property in suit including those which are covered by the sale deeds in favour of the alienes to Seshiah within one month therefrom. [541D E; 542A B] 2:2 The compromise is genuine and lawful and the same has to be acted upon. [542C D] 3.1 The alienees shall deliver vacant physical possession of that property by 30th April, 1991, to Seshamah within a period of one month from today. If possible, the trial court may appoint an Commissioner and taken police help in executing this decree and such costs shall ultimately he borne by Seshaah within two months therefrom. The alienee will deliver vacant actual possession of his property by 31st May, 1991. [543E] 3:3 In view Of the fact, that there has been a allegation of payments of Rs, 1 lakh, to SudarshanGupta which we had not investigated, and to met the further allegations that some improvement have been effected to the properties which too they were covered by sale deeds, the security furnished in the trial Court shall stand discharged and the alienation will form part Of the order for disposal of the Special leave petition.

Section 49 of the , provides that when a person is entitled to any of the benefits provided by the Act, he shall not be enti tled to receive any similar benefit admissible under the provisions of any other enactment. The question for consideration in these appeals was whether the benefits available under the Act in the matter of grant of sick leave are such as to justify the rejection of the workmen 's demand and the setting aside of the Tribunal 's awards in that respect. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) It is not necessary, in the circumstances of the case, to award the benefit of the sick leave with retro spective effect from January 1, 1975 in the case of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It appears, however, that it was not necessary for the Tribunal to award such a benefit at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. The other question regarding the adequacy of sick Leave has been examined by this Court in Technological Institute of Textiles vs Its Workmen and others (2) and it was held as follows with specific reference to the first proviso to section 49 of that Act according to which a person qualified to claim sickness benefit is not entitled to the benefit for an initial waiting period of two days except in the cases of continuous illness of the nature mentioned therein, "With regard to sick leave, the argument on behalf of the appellant was that the Tribunal should not, in any view of the matter, have given the benefit Of 7 days sick leave and that the workmen did not deserve anything more than sickness benefit for the first two days also. [864C D] (2)(a) The Tribunal has cor rectly examined the controversy and given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit. Such a leave could not be categorised as privilege leave as, by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the ease of actual illness certified by registered medical practitioners. It is well settled that where a person was entitled to sickness benefit, he should not be entitled to it for the initial waiting periods of two months except in case of continuous sickness certified at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sickness for which the sickness benefit was last paid. [874D E] (b) The question regarding adequacy of the Sick leave with retrospective effect from 1st January, 1975, in a given case, has been considered by this court in Technologists Institute of Textile Industry vs Its workmen and others, ; , referred to. (c) It would be permissible for the Court to award a lesser amount than that which was awarded by the Tribunal. [884E F] (3)(a). In the instant case, the Tribunal has come to the conclusion that the benefit cannot b.e said to be adequate for, it works out to about half the average average wage of a workman, and even that amount is not admissible for the second two days of sickness except in this case of an actual sickness Certified by a Registered medical practitioner.[884A B] (c ) The Tribunal had cor rected under a mistaken impression of the sickness benefits which the Act allowed for, as has been shown, it does not deal with all aspects of demand for sickness benefit and does not, at any stretch, provide that the grant would cease to apply when the benefits of the Act became available to the workmen. [894G H] (d) The award in the instant cases was made effective from the date of its commencement. It was not under a mistake of law or on account of an error apparent on the face of the record. The Tribunal, therefore, had correctly considered the matter and given sufficient reasons for awarding the benefit to the sick workmen also.

The appellant who was an Advocate of the High Court of Bombay had a standing of about thirty years. The grounds were not vague and no particulars of the activities alleged to have been carried on by him were given, viz., the particulars such as the length of period for which the petitioner is alleged to has carried on the so called espionage activities or the details of financial aid received by him or the names of persons aiding the said petitioner or any details of intelligence allegedly collected by him and made available by him to the Portuguese Government. The High Court rejected this contention holding that the grounds were vague requiring some clarification. Held, that the right of the detenue to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest cannot be said to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. If the appellant bad exercised his right to ask for particulars, at the time, from the detaining authority there can be no doubt that he would have been furnished then the very information which has been supplied in paragraph 12 of the Under Secretary 's affidavit in answer to para 15(g) of the appellant 's petition, both of which have been already set out above. A faint suggestion has been made in the course of the arguments before this Court that the decision not to disclose particulars is mala fide and that such mala fides has to be imputed in a case where no particulars are at all furnished. It is unnecessary, therefore, to deal with this question with a theoretical contention as to whether or not article 22 (6) of The Constitution overrides the constitutional right to be afforded a proper opportunity of representation. Such a contention as regards the mala fide exercise of the power is untenable in the present case having regard to the nature of the activity imputed to the appellant, it will enable him to present to the Advisory Board his difficulties in making a proper representation and to convey to it a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act for their own information and consideration. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have impede his constitutional rights of representation guaranteed by article 22.

Rule 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, provides that when after considering the reports on an officer 's misconduct, the Central Government is satisfied or the C in C is of the opinion that the trial of the officer by a General Court Martial was inexpedient or impracticable but considers the further retention of the said officer in the service as undesirable, the C. in C shall communicate the view of the Central Govern ment or his views, as the case may be, to the officer together with all reports adverse to him and he shall be called upon to submit his explanation and defence. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground inter alia that r. 14 of Army Rules 1954 was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that r, 14 of Defence Rules 1954, was ultra void as it violated articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the constitution. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant Union of India that the expression "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 of the read with r.14 of the Defence Rules, 1955, means removal of a person from the service of persons subject to this Act. HELD : (i) The words "subject lo the provisions Of this Act and such rules, the rules made thereunder may provide for (a) the removal, retirement, release or discharge from the services of persons under the Act; (b) the rule making power to remove an officer without being tried and convicted by court martial was in derogation of section 45 of the . Rule 14 is such a rule : it is, therefore, not ultra vires. The two sections 19 and 46 of the Act are mutually exclusive. [449 B C] (ii) There can be no valid rule where under, subject to the other provisions of the , the Central Govt may remove a personfrom the service. Under section 19(2)(a), the rules are such a Rule : it was, therefore not ultra within the meaning of article 14 or 19(6). [449 C D] (iii) The word "subject" occurring therein in section19 makes section 19 subject to section 45, and the Central Gover nment has thus no power to removed an officer from service in derogation Of the provisions contained in section 45.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of tea. It had been assessed to octroi duty under r. 21(b) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, for consumption, use or sale therein and at such rates as may be decided by it but not below the minimum and maximum rates specified in columns 2 and 3, respectively of Schedule 1 annexed to that Part, which were imported into the octroi limits for consumption and use or sell. The appellant company challenged the validity of r. 22 on the ground (1) that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limit fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r, 21; and (2) that the levy of octroi duty from April 1, 1963, was not validly levied by the Panchayat as it had failed to fix the octroi rates in accordance with law. Held: (i) The Standing Committee inspected the premises of the Company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. The Standing committee inspected the godowns of the company but in its order they had given very clear scantky facts. They did not say that the tea was crushed, processing or treating chemically and had acted contrary to the principles of natural justice on an assumption that the formalities contemplated by law were complied with. (ii)The Standing Committee was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits.

Section 12(6) of the , provides for commencement and conclusion of conciliation proceedings under section 20 but the first sub section of section 20 deals with what are called utility services and sub section 2 of that section provides as to when the conciliation proceedings conclude. (2) A conciliation proceeding shall be deemed to have concluded in the case where a settlement is arrived at, when a memorandum of the settlement is signed by the par ties to the dispute; (b) where no settlement is reached, when the report of the Conciliation Officer is received by the appropriate Government or when the Report of the Board is published under section 17, as the case may be; or (c) when a reference is made to a Court, Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal under section 10 during the pendency of conciliation proceeding. All conciliation proceedings before a conciliation officer or a Board or of any proceeding before a Labour Court or Tribunal orNational Tribunal in respect of an industrial dispute, no employer shall: (a) in regard to any matter connected with the dispute, alter to the prejudice of the workmen concerned in such dispute, the conditions of service applicable to them immediately before the commencement of such proceedings; or and (b). for any misconduct connected with a dispute, discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, any workman concerned in that dispute, save with the express permission in writing of the authority before which the proceeding is pending. Section 33(1) provides that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if proceedings are not closed but are carried on, as they were in the present case, or if the Conciliation officer does not make his report within 14 days he may be guilty of a breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b) of that Act. Held, further, that on this interpretation the conciliation proceeding could be prolonged much beyond what was contemplated by the Act and the termination would depend upon how soon a report is received.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the . The grounds stated that there was indiscriminate firing on 24th December, 1985 on Katras Coal Dump and the petitioner started indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendestine business of coal to establish the criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers, customers and passers by of the area. In those circumstances it appears that the grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. It, however, appears that after the order of detention was passed and before the actual service of the said order, the petitioner was taken into custody. From the affidavit of the District Magistrate it does not appear that either the prospect of immediate release of the detenu or other factors which can justify the detention of a person in detention were properly considered in the light of the principles noted in the aforesaid decision and particularly in the decisions, in Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate Etah and others, though there was a statement to the effect that the petitioner 's brother and the Petitioner had already surrendered in respect of the criminal charge against him. In these circumstances it cannot be said that either of the prospect or the question that the said detenu might be released or that there were such a possibility of his release, was taken by the detaining authority properly and seriously before the service of order there was no proper consideration of the fact that the detenu was in custody of that there had been any real danger of his being released. The continued detention of the petitioner under the Act is not justified. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of him being released, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised. In the instant case when the actual order of the detention was served upon the detenu, the detenu remained in jail. There is no indication that this factor or the questions that the aforesaid detenu might have been released were taken into consideration by the Detaining Authority properly and thoroughly before the Service of the impugned order was passed but at the time of the service, there was nothing to indicate that either either the possibility of immediate releasing of the detained person or other circumstances which could justify the detaining detention of another person in custody were properly consider ed in the context of the relevant factors. The order of preventive Detention when it was passed was not invalid and on relevant considerations, the service Of the order was not on proper consideration. It may be mentioned that in the petition it is nowhere stated that the detaining Authority had since been released orthat the prospect o immediate release was properly and with seriousness considered by the Government properly and severely before the services of the same order and public order was the price which the democracy in this country extracts from the public officials in order to protect the fundamental freedoms of our citizens. In this case there were indications that transfer of the Petitioner from one prison to another was considered but the need to serve the detention order while he was in jail, was not properly considered by him in the eye of the law and particularly when there was any real likelihood of his released, and the detenu could not have been put into preventive custody. Therefore, though the order is set aside, it may be reconsidered by the appropriate authority in accordance with the law.

Section 28 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the security of any article, ornament or both unless authorised by the Administrator so to do, (a) carry on business as a money lender or banker on the Security of any articles, or ornament, or both, (b) permit any other person to carry On money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carried on business, as such dealer. Section 28 confers power on the Administrator in the matter of granting or renewing a license to a dealer. The main object in putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. In other words, the various restrictions that have been put on the activities of the traders doing business in gold will have to be viewed from the aforesaid perspective. Therefore, in our view the objective, the policy and the Scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator while exercising his discretion under that section. The High Court struck down the aforesaid provision only on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been 954 provided by reference to which the power conferred upon the administrator could be exercised and that the section confers an absolute arbitrary, uncanalised powers without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The policy and object of the enactment and the schemes affords sufficient guidelines to the administrator in the matters of exercising his discretionary power under that Section. [954 F] (2) While conferring power on an Administrator in a matter of grant or renewal of a license, the unamended section does not impose any blanket or 956 absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on moneylending, banking and any other trade in the said premises in that behalf is not absolute in as much as the Administrator can authorise the third person to do business in that licensed premises of the dealer and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy, and purposes of the statute and by the prime consideration that circumvention Of the other provision of the act shall not be premitted. [1054 G H] (3) The object, the scheme and the object of enacting the Act along with the need to ensure speedy enforcement of the provisions of section 5(1) of the , requires more than sufficient guidance in the mater of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under section 5 (1). [1055 C D] (4) While granting or renew a license under section 28, the Administrator is required to have regard to the policy or purposes of that Act in making his orders.

The appellants claimed that they had acquired title by adverse possession prior to 1 1 1929, but the lower appellate Court found that "it was evident from the very beginning, Pachai Kandai Udayavar and his family had been claiming beneficial interest in the property and they were not holding the same as managers of the trust. In regard to the third point based on the appellants ' claim that they acquired title through adverse possession, the lower Appellate Court found: (1) that the properties belonged to the temple; (2) that it was transferred by a previous manager; and (3) that in cases falling under article 134 B, the transfer made by the manager of a Hindu endowment is challenged by his successor on the ground that it belongs to himself considerations which would govern the application of limitation are substantially different; and in such a case, the transfers being void ab initio, the possession of the transferee is adverse from the date of the transfer. HELD: (i) The question as to whether on facts proved in this case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed from office by other persons who were acting as de facto managers of a religious endowment on the basis that it belonged to him and not to the religious endowment, is a mixed question of fact and law, and the High Court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that the title of the temple had not been lost by adverse Possession before the suit was filed. The question whether the facts proved did not show that the alienor disposed of all the property or left the village ' but also that for the last 25 years or so, the management has been taken over by other person who are acting as a de facto manager of the Temple de jure, has not been discussed by the High court. [410 D E] (ii) The High Court had relied on the fact that the property belonged to 'the temple; that they have been transferred for valuable consideration; and so, it thought that the plea of adverse possession could not be sustained. If that be so, there was no escape from the conclusion that more than 12 years had elapsed since the date when the removal of the previous Manager who transferred the properties in question; and, therefore, if a suit were brought by respondents 1 to 3 on the date on which they were appointed trustees by respondent No. 1 on the relevant date, it would not be affected by the provisions of article 134B.

The appellant firm was granted a licence for exhibition of cinematographs in the premises known as Apsara Theatre, Gandhi Nagar, Jammu. On April 27, 1979, a suit was instituted against Ved Gupta and seven others by seven of the partners including Krishan Kumar for a declaration that the Cinema licence dated July 22, 1969 issued by the District Magistrate, Jammu was the property of the firm Apsra Theatre and for a prohibitory injunction restraining them from interfering in any manner with the running of the cinema by the plaintiffs and also for a mandatory injunction restraining defendants 1 to 7, namely, Shri Ved Gupta, who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsaara Theatre by the proceedings of his predecessor dated December 29, 1977 which was confirmed in appeal by the State Government and which had acquired finality between the parties by reason of the dismissal of the writ petition and the Special Leave Petition by the High Court and Supreme Court respectively. The District Magistrate rejected the said request by a detailed order dated April 21, 1979 holding that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely Shri VedGupta, who was held responsible under the Act and the Rules for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the Licence and answerable to the licensing authority for all commissions and omissions in the Cinema premises, he may be saved from any prosecution or other action under law in the capacity of licensee of the Theatre in respect o any illegal acts or offences committed by others in the said premises. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that no notice or hearing had been given to the partnership firm before the order was passed and since it is only the licensee who is held responsible, under the provisions of the Act, and the rules for due observance with all its terms and Conditions of the licences and answerable in the Theatre premises, the impugned order was void and in violation of the principles of natural justice. In appeal to this Court by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the District magistrate had no power under the Rules to make such an order; (ii) the licensing Authority had no jurisdiction to suspend the licence; (iii) since the said procedure has not been followed by the Licensing Authority, the order passed by him directing suspension of cinema shows in the theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The licensing authority had no powers under the statute or the Rules, to make an order. Proceeding on that premise, the learned Acting Chief Justice has said that under the circumstances of the case, the power to suspend a licence is conferred only by Section 6 F of the , as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the section are present, the licensing authorities had no authority to suspend or cancel the licence. The only other reason stated by the learned Chief Justice for quashing the District Collector 's order is that the District Judge had no competence under the law or the rules to make any such an Order. Proceeding On that premise the learned acting Chief Justice had said that Under the provisions Of the Act the power of suspension of a licence was conferred only on Section 6F of the . The only another reason stated in the impugned judgment for quashing of the District Court 's Order is that, the District judge has no jurisdiction under the .Act or the Rule to make the order. proceeding on that ground, the High court had said, that under section 6 F, the powers to suspend and cancel a licence are conferred only only by section 6F as one implied in the wider power of revoked and unless there is mention at all of the partner or its partners.

The appellants, who had migrated to Pakistan, were declared by a notification dated 12 9 1951 issued under section 7 of the , as evacuee property, and under section 8(1) of the Act, they became vested in the respondent as the Custodian for the State. On 13 2 1954 the appellants appeared before the respondent, and contended that he had no auth ority to issue the notice in question under section 12, and that it was therefore illegal. Held: (i) The rights of the appellants in so far as they related to the purchase by them of the mills and the factory in question were left open to the determination of the appropriate authorities, and there was no warrant for imposing a further limitation on that section, to cancel the agreement to sell the mills or the factory to them, which was one of the matters contained in cl. (b) of section 12 as it now stands, the Custodian had the power under section 10 to cancel leases created not merely by the evacuees but also by himself. The notice in terms refers firstly to the lease which it is proposed to cancel, and secondly to the movables in respect of which certain directions were given. In their petition under article 226, it was the validity of the notice, Exhibit C, with reference to these two matters that the appellants challenged. Held, (i)(a) The right of the Custodian to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof is unqualified and absolute and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". (b)(c) Under the section as it stood even before the amendment, but it was not put forward at any stage prior to the bearing of this appeal and that by itself would be sufficient ground for declining to entertain it which it may be noted is now sought to be raised by a supplemental proceeding under Order 16, rule 4 of the Supreme Court Rules.

The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh, was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March, 1963 and was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalized by the Sub Divisional Officer on 5th May, 1976. In the ultimate analysis the Member of the Board found that there was a gross and patent illegality in the order of the SubDivisional Officer and, consequently set aside the order dated 6th September, 1976 as well as the order passed by the Revenue Appellate Authority dated 14th April, 1975 directing that the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1955 and not according to the new law i,e.Act of 1955. The Sub Divisional officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 5th July, 1976 held that Surendrapal Singh (appellant) aged 12 years was a minor daughter of Raghubir singh and used to 725 study in Punjab and further held that the land in possession of RaghubirSingh was ancestral. Aggrieved by the said order of remand, Raghubir Singh filed an appeal before the Revenue Board for Rajasthan. However, the member of the board came to the conclusion that Surendra Pal Singh (Appellant) was born on 14st March, 1962 and was not 13 years old when the Ceiling proceedings were finalised by the sub Divisional Officer. The Board of Revenue held that there is a gross or patent illegality on not merely ignoring the law but also ignoring the directions of the Government itself. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that no appeal having been filed by the State from the order, the Board of the Revenue could not, while hearing the revision petition filed by Raghubir Singh set aside that part of the subDivisional Officer 's order which had gone against the State and in his favour. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: (1) The Board has general powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts. But subsection(2) made it clear that this superintendence would not be construed as giving to the High Court any jurisdiction to question any judgment of any inferior court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. Section 224 of the Act of 1950 is similar to section 107 of the Govt. of India Act, 1915 and there is no provision like sub section (2) of section 224 of Government of India Rules, 1935 in the Act in the State Government of Rajasthan Act, 1935. [723D E] (2)(a) The SubDivisional officer has power of superintendence over all subordinate revenue courts and it does not apply to judicial proceedings. It is clear from the language of Section 221 of the U.P. Land Revenue Act that the Board 's Revenue has general power of supervision and control and superintendence over subordinate revenue Courts and it did not apply for judicial proceedings.[723E] (b) The High court also took the view that it was not correct to say that section 9 is limited to the executive control and supervision of the Boards over subordinate Revenue courts and, therefore, it could not make use of its powers of jurisdiction of superintendence & control and the order Of the Board could not be held proper with reference to Section 9 of the Land Revenue Revenue Act. [758E F] (c) The sub Divisional officer committed the grave illegality on ignoring the fact that the board had appellate jurisdiction and it could never, while considering the revision application filed by M/s. Raghubir Singh and his son Surendrapal singh constituted one unit and not two units and the case was remanded to Sub Divisional Magistrate, Hanumapur for de novo determination of the ceiling areas for the appellant in law.

The Orissa High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the law reports published by it were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and that the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by him on the basis of the recommendations of Justice Palekar was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The law reports which are being published by the Ist Respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the First respondent in their production or publication of the said law reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Government on the ground that they contain information about the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested. [781E F] 2. The expression `newspaper ' as defined in the Act includes not merely `public news ' but also `comments on public news and information. It is significant that the expression `Newspaper' is defined by section 2 (b) to mean any printed periodical work containing public news or comments on public News and includes such other class of printed periodical worked as may, from time to time, be notified in this behalf by the State Government in the Official Gazette. The Act in question is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of the newspaper establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the statute the one which advances the object of the act and is in favour of the employee for whose benefit the Act is passed has to be accepted. [780D E] 3. The question whether a law journal Cuttack Law Times, which was not a newspaper because according to it the necessary pre requisite of a periodical in order to make it a newspaper was that it should contain mainly publicnews or comments upon public news, and that books containing authoritative reports for future reference could, by no means, be said to contain news so as to become newspapers. [779E] 4. The word `new ' is defined in section 2 of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955, as any working journalist, and includes any other person employed to do any work in, or in relation to, any newspaper establishment. The appellant was a licensee of the respondent. The agreement was described as an agreement of 'leave and licence ' entered into between the respondent on the one hand and the appellant on the other wherein the respondent had been described as the licensee and the recitals therein recite that the licensor was seized and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as the monthly tenant of the workshop premises situated at 231, Ripon Road, Cooperative Building, Bombay, being the premises in dispute, and whereas the licensee had approached the licensor to allow him to occupy and use the said premises for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years and whereas, the licensor had agreed to allow the licensee to use the premises under the leave and licence of the licensor for a further period of 5 years from 1st September, 1965 till 31st August, 1970, that agreement was being executed. It was stated in the plaint that the respondent was a tenant and having found that the period of licence had come to an end, he passed an order of eviction against the appellant. The High Court allowed the revision on the ground that there was no subsisting agreement for licence on the 1st February, 1973 as there was nothing on record to show that after 31st March, 1966 the leave & licence agreement between the parties was renewed or any fresh agreement was entered into. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: (1) In view of the intention of the parties in the document and the facts and circumstances of this case it was a licence and not a lease. good deal of submission was made before us that if it was an agreement for leave and Licence then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the Court had to jurisdiction, and there was an estoppel. [231B C] (2) In order to go back to the findings of the High Court on the question whether the respondent is a licensee or a tenant, it must be shown by long process of reasoning, and the High court should not exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution. [232D E] (3) The background of the entire document indicates that the appellant was in occupation of the premises on 1st January, 1973 under a subsisting licence. good dealing of submission is made before this Court that if the exclusive possession to which a person was entitled under an agreement with a landlord was coupled with an interest in the property, the agreement would be construed not as a mere licence but as a lease; and in any event by filing the application for eviction the appellant licensor had granted an implied licence to the respondent licensee to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. [230E F] (4) In the instant case, it is a licence which was not put an end to by the appellants and that in any eventuality by filing of the application seeking eviction the licensor has granted an express or implied licence, to the appellant licensee to continuance in possession until a decree for eviction was made in his favor. [233B C D] (5) In this view of this matter this appeal must fail as there is no error apparent on the face of the record, the error if any has to be discovered by long processes of reasoning and theHigh Court should not exercising jurisdiction under article 227 of Constitution.

The covenanting State of Rajasthan was to provide for the continuance of laws in the covenanting States till such time as they were modified by the new State. The agreement provided that the assets and liabilities of the Covenanting States were to be the assets, and liabilities arising from the existence of those laws. On January 26, 1950, the Government of Rajasthan issued a notification under article 295(2) of the Constitution exempting certain territories from the operation of the covenanted State till such date as they formed part B State of Madhya Pradesh on account of political changes to which we have already referred. It was contended for the appellant that even if there was any liability of the former State of Dholpur to; refund the amount of tax collected in advance for no export was made, that liability did not devolve on the Part B State as it emerged on January 26 1950. Held, that article VI of the agreement was not a law but only a law which clearly applied to the Mills and it was held that there could be no question of recognition by the Union of the right to exemption, if any under the agreement with the Ruler of the erstwhile Jodhpur State. It is well settled that clauses in treaties entered into by sovereigns of independent States whereunder sovereignty in territories passed from one to the other providing for the recognition by a new sovereign of the existing rights of the inhabitants of those territories must be regarded as invested with the character of an act of State and no claim based thereon could be enforced in a court of law. It follows therefore that when the new state continued all the old laws till they were repealed or altered, recognised that it was liable in the same way as would have been the merging State if there had been any liability on the merger of the old law which would affect the liability or even otherwise that law would prevail and the liability may disappear provided the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to transportation for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to transportation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the death sentences on the three appellants, should be maintained and that those of the other two should be commuted to transportation; and (ii) there is no evidence that any one knew who the assailants were and that therefore the accusation made against the accused was a subsequent concoction and that it was for that reason that they thought they must have joined in the attack and so had added that detail to their story. HELD: (i)(a) The sentence should be reduced to transportation in these two cases mainly because of the difference of opinion in the High Court, not only on the question of guilt but also on that of sentence. [446 B] (b) There is no reason to depart from this practice in this case and so reduce the sentences of death in the case of Bhilia and Tukia to transportation, for life because of section 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and it was usual not to impose the death penalty unless there are compelling reasons. [404 C D] (c) There was evidence that all three lived together and that one was a younger brother and the other a tenant of the appellant in question. In the present case, the facts disclosed do not warrant an inference of common intention in Pandurang 's case. That leaves the question whether Tukaram is proved to have done anything except be present and even if it be accepted that Nilia aimed a blow, at Ramchander 's thigh be was so half hearted about it that it did not even hit him; and in Pandurang vs The State of Bombay, ; , followed. (ii)(a). There was no evidence to show that any stick blows were found on the body and that none on the part of the two who did the actual murder. There is also some vague evidence to the effect that there had once been a dacoity at Ram chander ''s house and that he suspected "the accused" and reported them to the police who arrested them, but nothing came of it and they were later released. [405 G H] (iii) The High court was right in holding that section 378 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not abrogate or modify that provision. But when appellate Judges, who agree on the questions of guilt differ on thatof sentence, it is usual not always to impose a death penalty until there are strong reasons. But if appellate judges, who disagree on the point of guilt, differ on the same of sentence, they are bound to impose death penalty if there are cogent reasons. If the law directs otherwise, it must remain, a matter of discretion unless the law requires otherwise. But where appellate Judges agree on that question of conviction, it may be usual not not to imposing the death Penalty unless there is compelling reasons; but when appellate judges differ on this point of sentence they are equally bound to follow the practice in the matter and so reduced the sentences awarded by them.

The appellant Corporation issued a notice to the respondent Corporation for the payment of Rs. 1,00,000/ towards premium payable by the deceased on 11th January, 1961. The said notice was accepted by the Corporation without any demur or qualification and that in any event the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality, if any, of sending communication of acceptance of the proposal. The respondent Corporation filed a suit against the appellant Corporation for recovery of Rs 1,50,000/- on the ground that there was a concluded and valid insurance contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11 th January, 1962 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the appellant. The Trial Court held that there had been a concluded contract of insurance between the appellant and the Life Insurance Corporation and therefore it was the case of the plaintiff respondents that with full knowledge of the completion of all preliminaries, the Corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards the first premium and therefore there was no concluded contract between them. The High Court also held that the other averments in the claim that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the Corporation that the payment would amount to the acceptance of proposal were not established and even if such a representation was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules the payment could never amount to acceptance of a proposal if the proposal was not otherwise accepted. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The plea that Divisional Manager was the only authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf of the appellant corporation and secondly because 359 there was assurance on behalf by the field Officer and local agent to the deceased that the payments would amount towards the premium could never be accepted firstly because factually it was not proved and secondly Because there was nothing to show the position alleged by the plaintiffs respondents that the amounts paid were appropriated towards the premiums and the want of any further action to be done by the respondent did not itself create a contract of Insurance between the appellants and the life insurance Corporation. The allegation that there were assurance on the part of the field officers and local agents to the appellant that the amount paid was appropriated towards premium and the said premium amount would amount in those circumstances, cannot also be accepted merely because factually the it was never proved and thirdly because 359 the there was some evidence that such could have been the deposition in law. [359H; 358A B] 2. The contention that Divisional manager was the sole authority to receive a proposal for Rs.1,50.000/ has not been specifically taken in this written statement. It is significant that the case set out in the plaint and the basis of the claim made in the notices sent to the Corporation was not that the proposal sent by the proposer was as a matter of fact accepted by it and like 358 other contracts, the contract of policy was complete by offer and acceptance. The evidence on record in this case does not insist on the full repayment of the sum paid and counsel on behalf for the Life insurance Corporation has stated that they would accept if half of what has been received by the respondents, namely principal together with interest is paid back to the appellants, namely, principal together alongwith interest is payable back to them.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business of mining and selling coal. The company had its registered office at Madras in which it was engaged in the manufacture and sale of coal. It had also its registered offices at Madras, Madras, Bombay, Madras and Madras. In the course of its business, the appellant sold coal to the respondent for a sum of Rs. 1,00,000. The respondent filed an application under section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935 for grant of interim injunction in respect of the said amount. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the suit was not maintainable since the decision on the issue did not finally dispose of the dispute between the parties. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that an order granting interim injunction "is a final order" as far as this Court is concerned, determining the rights and liabilities of the parties within this lit or proceeding, which is independent though ancillary to the suit", and that an interlocutory judgment even if it decides an issue or issues without finally determining the right and liability of the party in dispute in the suit or proceeding from which appeal has arisen, is not a judgment under article 133(1)(c) since the controversy between the two parties when the complaint in respect o offences under sections 467 and 468 read with section 114 I.P. Code was concerned merely with an order passed by the High Court which maintained the order of the Additional Sessions Judge that a complaint under section205 read with Section 114 I P.C. could be filed against the appellant. HELD: (i) The expression "final order" in article 133 (1)(b) means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. [934 C] (ii) An order passed in appeal which does not finally disposes of a suit or proceedings and leave the rights in disputes have to be determined, the order is interlocutory. Code. This Court held (Bachawat & Mitter JJ., dissenting) that the cause of action was personal to the insolvents and did not vest in the assignee, and accordingly they set aside the decree and remanded the suit for trial. The order refusing to grant an interim injunction did not determine the rights or obligations of the Parties in relation to the matter in dispute In the present case, the plaintiff 's suit as a result of the order passed on the question did not decide any important point or even a vital issue in the case. If it did not, and the suit/ proceeding was a live one, yet to be tried, the Order was held not to be final within (1) (2) E.R. In Mohammad Amin Brothers 's case(3) an issue was decided by the trial court in a petition for winding up of a Company as to the maintainability of a claim for recovery of income tax dues. The Court in that case was concerned only with an interlocutory order, but if after the order was made, the suit is still left alive and has got to be try in the ordinary way, no finality could attach to the order. [1034 C D] (iii) An Order passed by a High Court in an appeal which did not ultimately dispose of a case or proceeding may be deemed final for the purposes of article 133 of the Constitution, under section 109 Code of Civil Procedure or section 205(1) of the Govt. of India act, 1935 if it amounts to a final decision on that rights and obligations of parties for determination in the suits or proceedings from which appeals have arisen, are not final within the meaning of article 134(1).
