The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the Panchayat Samiti in 1963 long before the Amending Act came into force on June 13, 1973. On March 14, 1975 a resolution was passed by respondent 3 regularising the post of Head Clerk. On April 1, 1975, the appellant was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 13 of the Amending act provided that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1 1973 shall continue to service on the same terms and conditions on which they were employed by the panchayat Samiti, until they are absorbed in Government service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. Acting in pursuance of the provision of section 14(4) of the Act, the Government of Haryana notified the absorption of the appellant as a Clerk. The Amending Act received the assent of the Governor 736 on April 25, 1973 and was published in the Haryana Gazette on June 12, 1973, which was published by the Haryana Government on July 13, 1974. Sections 35(1) and (3) were amended by section 14 of the amending Act of 1973. Section 14(5) provided that a Panchayat Samitis may employ such servants as it may consider necessary for the efficient performance of the duties imposed upon them by the Act rules or bye laws made thereunder or by any other law for the time being in force, and for such other duties and functions as may, be assigned to them by Panchayat Samiti from time to time. Section 35(3) which dealt with the conditions of service of the Government servants allotted to the Panchayat Samitis, was amended by Section 14 of Act 1973. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court praying that he should be absorbed as a head clerk in any event. The writ petition having been dismissed by the High court, the appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to be consider for promotion but, whether the Panchayat Parishad had the right to appoint him to the post as aHead Clerk on the date on which it purported to do so. Clearly, it had fortified that right on June 14, 1973 when the Amending Acts came into operation. It could not, therefore, have appointed the appellant to the posts of a Head clerk prior to his absorption in Government Service until he was absorbed in government service or retired in such way as may not be prescribed by law. The appointment of the appellants to the office of a head Clerk being without the authority of law, the government was not bound to absorb him in the post on which he purported to doing so. [775C D] (2) It could only have appointed a person who was in service at the commencement of Amending Act of 1972 on an Ad hoc basis or in April 1975 on a regular basis.

Their father Sardar Nand Singh was 42 330 found entitled to quasipermanent allotment of 40 standard acres. The ground on which the appellants ' application was rejected by the Deputy Custodian General was that his jurisdiction to revise the order has been taken out by virtue of the provisions of , (44) of 1954 and the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of sections 12(2), 19 and 19 of the Act on the ground that their jurisdiction to revised the order had been wrongly taken away by virtue Of the provisions contained in section 8 of the , and (5) that the notification under section 12(1) of the with respect to any property or class of property would be to divest the Custodian completely of his right in the property flowing from section 8. A suit for possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it was filed on the basis that the appellant as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties of the dera at Landeke, that the defendant was unlawfully claiming to be the mahant of the said Dera, and entitled to management of the properties. The trial court held that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Dass, as his Chela "inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a dispute is raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. The High Court held that since there was no certainty as to the person who would become the mahants by election, that it was uncertain on the death or for any other reason. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. A suit cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest of a party in the subject matter of the suit has devolved upon another during the pendency of the litigation but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of interest of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, rule 10 and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death orfor any other reasons. It was, however, contended on behalf of the respondent that the suit was for possession and management of properties appertaining to it by the appellant purporting to be his de facto mahant against Som Dass as de jure mahant. The fact that it is after Som Dass died that Shiam Das was elected to be a mahant could make no difference when we are dealing with the question whether the interest in the said subject matter had devolved upon him. [412C D] 2. In Roshan Lal vs Kapur Chand, the Court took the view that devolution of the interest was in the same representative capacity that the appeal was sought to be continued under Q. 10(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and that there was a devolution by virtue of law 490 or custom that there would be devolution of any interest during the proceedings of a suit and, therefore, Order 22 rule 10 will apply (1). In Roshanlal vs Kapurchand, the Supreme Court took note of the fact that the subject matters of the suits were the interest o f Som Dass in the Dakhera and its properties and it devolved upon shiam Dass by virtue Of his election as mahant subsequent to the death. The Court said that where some of the trustees die or retire during the course of a litigation and new persons are elected to fill their place, it is a case of devolution of an interest during pendency of a proceeding and the elected persons can be added as parties under Order 22 Rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. [512D E] 3. The subject matter in the suit is the interest and management and the property appertaining to them by virtue o law 490, or custom, that there will be devolution on shiam Das by virtueof his election, as mahants of Dera after the lifetime of Som Chand Dass. And, as it was in a Representative capacity, that Som Dass was sued and as it is in the latter representative capacity,that the appeal could be continued by oragainst the person to or upon whom such interest has come or devolved. [612E F] 4.

The petitioners in these writ petitions were employees of the Government of Andhra Pradesh. They challenged the reduction of the age of retirement from 58 to 55 on the ground that it was unreasonable, arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India; that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that as a result of the increase in the age from 55 to 58 years in 1976, a vested right had accrued to the petitioners, which could be taken away, if at all, only from future entrants to the Government service; and that the decision of the State Government was bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of age of superannuation, like increased longevity. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which are relevant on the fixation of the ages of retirement, like increase longesvity; that in some States in India the age is 55 and not 58; the present decision was taken by the Government in order to fulfill its commitment that it will take welfare measures in orderto improve the lot of the common man, and. particularly, in order that to afford opportunities to qualified and talented unemployed youths whose number was increasing enormously due to expansion of educational facilities; that, the Government employees were stagnated in the lower positions due to the increase of age from55 to 58: and that, therefore, the present measure was intended to have a salutary effect on the creation of incentives to the deserving employees whose number had been increased disproportionously due by expansion of education from 55to 58 years; that it is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. No. The contention of the petitioners is that the proviso which conferred a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, cannot be amended so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be changed retrospectively so as not to take away rights which had already accrued to them; and, therefore violative of article 14 or Article 16 since it is neither arbitrary nor unreasonable in its circumstances. No case has been made out for increasing the ageof retirement from 55 To 58 years. The Government was therefore justified in its contention that arbitrary fixation of retirement age amounts to "removal" from service and is therefore violative Of Article 14 and Article 16, since it was not arbitrary and unreasonable in view of our conclusion that the reduction in the case is not hit by Article 14 orArticle 16, because it is no arbitrary or reasonable in the facts of the present case. [775C D] 1.2 The Government has acted unreasonably without giving any prior notice to employees which could have enabled him to arrange his affairs on their eve of superannuation; that by a notification dated September 17, 19,9 the recommendations of the one Man Pay Revision Commission were accepted by the State Govern ment and consequently, the age was raised to 58 with effect from October 29 l 979. The recommendation regarding increasing the Age of retirement was not accepted by Government initially because, it felt that raising the age Of retirement would reduce employment opportunities in the immediate future; that a vested rights had accrued on them, which would result in grave detriment to public services of the state; and That, the decision taken by Government is bad for the total non applications of mind. [76H; 77A] 1:3 The State Government is therefore justified In its contention, that the question as regards the age or retirement was a pure question of Governmental policy affording no cause of action to the petitioner to file the writ petition.

Section 9(1) of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973 provides that a dealer liable to pay tax under this Act, (a) purchases goods other than those specified in Schedule B; or (b) purchases any goods from any source in the State and uses them in the manufacture of any other goods and disposes of the manufactured goods in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce or in the Course of export out of the territory of India within the meaning of sub section (1) Of section 5 of the Central Sales Tax, Act 1956; or. (c) purchases other than Those specified in Schedules B and C except milk from any sources in the state and uses thereof in the manufacturing of goods specified in the Schedule B. Explanation 1 to section 9(3) provides that where a dealer who purchases them has claimed exemption under section 24(1), but is found not to have used the goods for the purposes speci fied therein i.e. for the manufacture or sale of guar gum and utensils where the purchase is exempt even if purchased by a registered dealer for the purpose of export within the ambit of sub s.(3) of section 5, he shall be levied, subject to the provisions of section 17, a tax on the purchase of such goods at such rate as may be notified under section 15. The High Court held that the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clauses (b), (bb) and (bb), later inserted with retrospective effect from 27.5.1971 would not include cases of despatches by a dealer of the said manufactured goods otherwise than through sale as, for example, by way, of stock transfer. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that section 9 (1)(b) exempts only sales made in the process of export outside the territory oi s 5(3), but does not tax purchases even in cases where the manufactured products are disposed of only by way 'pultimate sales falling under section 5(1). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The words "or despatches the manufactured articles to a place outside the State in any way otherwise than as by way o sale in t he course of export" in section 9 of the Act should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. This definition includes within the definition of 'turnover ' the purchase value of goods liable to tax under section 9 but, the goods presently in question are not laible to tax either u/s 9(i)(b), or section 6 or section 24 (3) on which the present argument on behalf o f the Revenue is based. [351B C] 2.1 The words 'disposes ' used in clauses (a), (ii) and.(bb) of sub Section (1 ) of section 9 should be read as including, within the definitions of "turnover ', the purchase price of goods which are sold by a manufacturer and, indeed, the assessees would have had to pay Tax on the sales made to them but for a claim for exemption under s 24. 31.3.1983 and their amendment in 1986 have also a bearing in the cases of raw materials purchased for manufacture of gugar gum, and utensils wherein the purchase was exempt even though purchased by registered dealer. [352D E] 2:2 The words, "or dispatches the goods to a places outside the state in any mode otherwise than under way of sales" occurring in clause(a)(i) should be construed as including cases of sales falling within section 5 (3), not only as contended for the assessees and held by us above but also on the hypothesis as to the invalidity of s 9(I)(b).

The appellant who was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947 continued to be the owners of the goods till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream, and so no tax was realisable on these sales in view of the provisions of article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. Held: (i) The words " a person" in section 10(b) are wide enough to include a person who has given such certificate under section 8(b). In the present sales the property in the goods passed to the buyers on shipment, that is, after they had crossed this frontier, the sales must be held to have taken place "in the course of export" and the exemption under article 286 (1)(a) will come into operation only if the goods were not 'despatched outside the State of Bombay within the prescribed period by anybody. A close examination of sections 8 and 10 justifies the conclusion that the Legislature was anxious to secure that the declaration as regards intention of the parties being despatched outside the state of Bombay should be carried out by despatch by " a registered registered dealer" to whom he sells the goods, but who is not a registereddealer, the certificate has not been complied with. It may well be that if at the time a declaration of intention is made in the certificate the purchasing dealer had the intention as stated and ultimately he sells to a person other than a registered manufacturer for despatch of the said goods outside the Province of Bombay, the purchasing dealers may not be liable for having made a false declaration. The words ' a person ' in section 8 have been furnished in respect of such goods and the purchase dealer does not show to the satisfaction of the Collector that the goods have been despatched by him or by a person to whom it has sold the goods to an address outside the province of Bombay. (ii)The word " a" used in section 9(b)(i) is wide enough so as to include persons who are not registered dealers as sufficient. (iii)If at the date when the declaration of intent was made in a certificate the purchaser has the intention that goods shall be the property of the licensee, and if ultimately the actual despatch is made by some person who is neither a registered owner, it cannot strictly be said that the declared goods purchased were intended for being despatched by the dealer to whom the certifying dealer has sold them. (iv)The words "a person " in section 12(b), are wide sufficient to include all persons who have given such certificates under sections 8(c) and 10(d). (v)If the time of the export should be interpreted as the time when the customs frontier is crossed, it will be unreasonable to think that the parties came to a special agreement that though the sales were on FOB contracts property in Bombay they would pass to the buyer at some point of time before shipment.

The appellant, who was married to the respondent, filed a petition under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 for a monthly allowance for the maintenance of herself and her child. The magistrate held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 400/ for the mother for their subsistence taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived, was high, and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appellant. This order was challenged before the Sessions Judge by the aggrieved husband who on a strange view of the law that the court under section125 had no jurisdic tion to consider whether the applicant was a wife, dismissed the petition in allowance of the appeal. The Sessions Judge held that there must be proof of neglect to maintain to attract s. 125 and his third contention was that there was a settlement by consent decree in 1962 whereby the appellant had transferred the suit premises, namely, a flat in Bombay to the appel lant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that he was a divorcee and awarded a monthly maintenance allowance of Rs 400/ per month for her subsistence taking into consideration the fact whether the cost had been paid before such order, (i) in the case where such sum was paid before the date on which such order was made; (ii) in any other case from the date of expiry of the period if any, for which maintenance has been actually paid by the husband to the woman; but if one were to locate a legal ground to raise The contention that the liability to pay maintenance had ceased on account of the payment of mehar money, it was section 127(3) (b) subserves the goal and relieves; the obligor, not pro tanto but wholly. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 In a case where the husband, by customary payment at the time of divorce, has adequately provided for the divorce, a subsequent series of recurrent does is 81 contra indicated and the husband liberated. The legal sanctity of the payments is certified by the fulfilment of the social obligation, not by a ritual exercise rooted in custom. If the first payment by way of meherhar or ordained by custom has a reasonable relation to the object and is a capitalised substitute for the order under section 127 not mathematically but wholly; but fairly then section 127 (3) subservies the goaland relieves. The obligor cannot claim under section 126(3)(b) absolution from this obligation under section 128 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. [81C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the consent decree of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all claims then available But here is a new statutory right created as a projection of public policy by the Code of 1973, which could not have been in the contemplation of the parties when in 1962, they entered into a contract to adjust their then mutual rights. No settlement of claims which does not have the special statutory right of the divorcee under section 124 can operate to extinguish that claim. Payment of mehahar money as a customary discharge, is within the cognisance of that provision. [82D E] 1:3 In the context of section 127 of the Code, it is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the Parties. There must be a rational relation between the sums so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance.

(1) The order dated 25th March, 1988 of the Collector is under challenge in this appeal. The same reads as follows: "Shri Raghu Nath Thakur S/o Late Gorakh Thakur, Village Repura, P.S. Puksha, District Samastipur had bid for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction on 27.3.88 and he as given the shop of Beni Country liquor shop held on 27th March 1988. After signing in Bandobasti Register he did not deposit dak amount. The name of Shri Raghu Nath Chauhan S/O Late Gorakh Ram Thakur, village Repura Pusa, Distt. Samasti is also placed in the black list for future under the orders passed by the Collector. " This order was passed pursuant to the order of the Commissioner. The letter dated 25.3,.88 states as follows:- "The Collector after perusal of the said office note passed order on 25.03.88 which is produced in verbatim below: Ist bidder chunki defaulter hai atah security prapt kar len tatha bhavishya ke liae Black list karen. " " Indisputably, no notice had been given to the appellant of the proposal of black listing the appellant. It was contended on behalf of the State Government that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In so far as the contention that there is no requirement specifically of giving a prior notice is concerned, the respondent is right. But it is an implied principle of the rule that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the PG NO 869 principles of natural justice. It has to be realised that black listing every person in respect of business ventures has civil consequence for the future business of the person concerned in any event. In this view of the matter, the last portion of the order directing that the appellant be placed in black list is set aside. So far as cancellation of the bid of the respondent was concerned, that is not affected. This order will however not prevent the State government or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps for blacklisting the appellant if the Government is so entitled to do so in accordance with law, i.e. giving the appellant due notice and an opportunity of making representation. After hearing the appellant, the State Govt will be at liberty to pass any order in accordance With law indicating the reasons therefor.

The appellant was the owner of a vacant piece of land with no title to the buildings standing on the site in item 17 (2) and measuring 41 grounds and 2005 sq. 534/66, the Court, on a perusal of the sale deed dated 30.7.53 filed by the LIC before it came to the conclusion that the buildings on the land leased under exhibit P 1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in respect of this premises also. The Rent Controller held that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibitP 1 was only a vacant site, the Rent Controller had no juris diction to fix the fair rent. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the tenants that the order of the Court of Small Causes in the earlier rent control proceedings deciding to the contrary and fixing the fair price of item 1 at Rs.994 p.m. should be completely ignored as an order passed totally without jurisdiction, though it has become final as be tween the parties? Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The question on which the jurisdiction of the civil court is excluded is only the determination as to the fair or standard rent for the premises. If, and only if, this relationship exists between the parties, the tenant will have to pass a decree in favour of the LIC on the basis of the fair rents fixed by the Rent controller. It will not be open to the civil Court to re determine the rent payable by the tenant to the landlord because that is a matter squarely and exclusively within the jurisdiction o the Rent Control ler under the Act. [549G H] (2)(a) In an application under section 4, the court of Small Cause has to decide: (i) whether the applicant is a tenant in or landlord of, the building and (ii) what the fair market rent is and then fades out of the picture. If the civil courts in this case had come to the finding that there was a relationship of landlord and a tenant and that t he LIC was not entitled to recover the rent from the tenants, it will have jurisdiction to entertain a suit by the defeated party; for such a suit would be barred by section 12(4) of the Act; (b) Whether the order in the previous proceedings is to be treated as an 570 order that is null and void or merely one that is valid until set aside, the answer has to turn on the true nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the Rent Controlling ler Under the Rent control Act, the question on Which the jurisdiction is excluded from the purview of the Civil Court 's jurisdiction as well as the provisions of the Acts. [552C D] (3)(a). In an appeal under section 12, the State contended before this Court that every refusal of a ryotwari patta by a Settlement Officer in an inquiry under section 11 involves a decision on his part that either the applicant was not a ryot or the land is not ryoti land; in the instant case it was the latter and such decision on the nature or character of the land had been given a finality under section 64 C which cannot be ques tioned in a court of law. [553H] (4)(b) In the instant cases, there is no doubt that, since an application for this purpose cannot lie except at the instance of a landlord or a tenant, the rent controller has to deal with this incidentally but this is not one of the direct issues before the Rent Controllers. If it and only, if, the relationship exists both the parties i.e. the former and the latter, theRent Controller steps in for a limited purpose to determine what thefair rent is or then fade out ofthe picture.

The petitioner was a respondent who had not appeared before the High Court and, therefore, could not be heard by us. The case now before us is governed by what was held by this Court in Shankariah 's case (supra) and on a failure to appreciate the facts of the case of the peti tioner respondent which is now before this Court, it was held that a person whose seniority is to be determined under Section 115 of the Act must be given an opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and order of the Mysore High Court, ^ HELD: (1) The respondents were entitled to an opportunity of making a representation with regard to the two points urged by the petitioner respondent before the final list was to be declared and published as a final list. [828G H] (2) It is not within the province of the Courts to lay down what are in the principles to be adopted for purposes of equation. If that is established, the decision of the authorities concerned will have to stand. But, once he has had that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority list.[828G] (3) The petitioner respondent Dr. R.D. Nanjiah and others similarly placed respondents before us have been unable to make out, in their petitions, any grounds for interference with the final gradation list on some such grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist.

The petitioners in both the writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. These licences were valid for a period of 12 months and they contained the following endorsement: "This licence in valid for import of items permissible to Export Houses under the Additional Licence category as per para 176 of Import Policy 1988 79 excluding those items which were banner in the policy for the period 1978 79 excluding Those items which have been specifically banned in the prevailing Import Policy, 1985 88, pursuant to and subject to the decision of the Supreme Court dated 5.3.1986 in M/s. Rajnikant Brothers case (supra) and the Export Houses who were issued Additional licences prior to April 1, 1988, on exports made during 1986 87 or earlier periods have been denied the facilities which have not been given to Export House who were issuing Additional licences on or after April 1 1988, under the Import & Export Policy 1978 91. The petitioners who were granted Additional licences to the extent of 33.33% of the f.o.b. value of the exports made them during the year 1977 78 cannot, therefore, be said to be persons similarly circumstanced as Export House which exported goods in the year 1987 88 and in subsequent years and obtain Additional licences for a much lesser value under the import Policy 1988 91 on the basis of exports made after 1986 87. On behalf of the petitioners it has been urged that under Import & export Policy 1978 79 Additional licences were to be given on the ground that they had been specifically prohibited in the prevalent Import Policy 197879 and the export Houses who would be granted Additional Licences prior to the date of import. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners have been granted Additional licence in pursuance of this Court 's order dated April 18, 1985 in Rajnkantikant Brothers, case (Supra) and had imported canalised items under the said licence. [236E F] 2.2 In other words, under Import and Export Policy 1988 89 Additional licences are to be granted on the strength of not foreign exchange earnings from the exports actually made and the value of such Additional licence is only 10 to 12% of net Foreign exchange earnings. The appellants therein had been granted additional licences in pursuance to this Court order dated 4.4.1985 in Raj nikant Brothers ' case ( supra). Since there has been relaxation in the matter of policy of canalisation of imports under sub para (4) of paragraph 215 in respect of Additional licences granted to Export houses under Import/ Export Policy, 1988 91, the petitioners are also entitled to a similar relaxation. [237B C] 3.1 Under the Import and Exports Policy 1978 80 Additional licences issued to the petitioners were valid only for a limited period of twelve months and the said period has expired during the pendency of these writ petitions. Since the matter has been pending in this Court and the Additional Licences issued to them have expired in the meantime, we consider it appropriate that the period of validity of the said licences should be extended so that the petitioners can avail the same and are able to import the goods which can be so imported under the prevailing import policy. [238D E] 3:2 In view of the fact that the matter had been pending before this Court since the Additional licences have expired during pendency of the writ petition, it is directed that the Period of validity shall be extended by six months from the date on which such extension is granted. The period of Validity of the Additional licence that has been granted to the petitioner under import and Export policy 1978 79 may be extended for so that they can avail of the same, and are unable to import goods which could be so import under the prevalent import policy 1988 91.

Section 4(4)(d) of the Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 provides for excise duty with reference to value of the excisable goods, while determining the value of such goods, the cost of packing which is returnable by the buyer to the assessee. The relevant provi sion of section 4 of the Act deals with the manner as to how the value is to be computed and section 4(5)(d)(i) stipulates that in cases where the goods are delivered at the time of removal in a packed condition, includes the cost cost of such pack ing which is of a durable nature and is returnable By the buyer, in respect of all other costs of packing, the costs shall be included in the assessable value of excisable goods. According to the learned Attorney General, since the Act provides for only one exception to this measure, namely, non inclusion of the cost price of such packing where the packing is durable in nature and are returnable by a buyer to him, in all other cases, the Cost of the packing would have to be included In the assessable Value of the goods. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The cost of the pack ing envisaged in section 4 (4)(D)(i), does not in clude within its ambit the cost for packing not incurred by the manufacturer when the packing was supplied by the seller and recovered from the buyer except where the pack is of durable character and ordinarily incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. Therefore, while generally the normal price for which the goods were sold at the factory gate is to a be taken as the assessable valuation, an addition thereto has to be made where, in addition to the price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which was intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placed the manufactured product on the Market. [785C D] 2. The "cost of such Pack ing" referred in section 3(4) (d)(ii) does not refer to the cost incurred by a manufacturer when he supplies the drums and charges the customers separately therefore, then, under section 4.(4)(e), the cost is only the "cost" incurred by him in respect for all other expenses of packing including those supplied by him. The expression "assessable value ' as interpreted in section before its amendment cou pled with the now well established position that the amended ment intended to make no change in this position, the use of the word "cost", rather than "value", the nature of the other payments referred to in sub clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that, while normally the normal prices for which goods are sold at a factory gate are to be takenas the assessable values, an add thereto has been made where in addition, to the value, the manufacturers levies a charged for the packaging which is intrinsically or inevitably incidental thereto placing the finished goods on market. In this view of the matter, I consider it unnecessary to discuss wider questions as to the circumstances in which the cost Of packing (primary or secondary) can at all enter into the determination of the 995 assessable value under section4(4). [786D E] Union of India & Ors. vs Godfrey Phillips, by the learned counsel for the assessee or as to correctness or other wise of the decision of this Court in Union of lndia & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant was sentenced to undergo R.I. for 15 months under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. PW 3, the Principal of the training School issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the PW 1, Venkataswamy, the canteen contractor as to why his licence for running the canteen should not be cancelled. This was on the basis of a complaint made by the appellant that the food served in the canteen was substand ard. The prosecution case is that the accused thereafter sent for PW 1 informed him that he would help him in restoring the licence and demanded a bribe of Rs. On 21.10,.1975, the appellant was stated to have pressed the demand to PW 1. PW 6 after drawing up a mahazar in the presence of PW 2, Jaganathan, Assistant of the Office of the Special Tehsildar Usilampatti directed PW 1 to give the notes to the appellant who received the same. The appellant produced the currency notes. The test was positive, the currency note found in his possession was the money returned by PW1, the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the appellant and the presumption, if any, arising under section 4(1) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act which has not been rebutted. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the appel lant and recorded the conviction. Before the High Court, thecontentions of the appellants were that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the 337 behest of the accused had not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient, the explanation offered by the appeli lant was probable and there is no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appellant. The High Court thought that though the conviction under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5 of the Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I. P.C., and section 4 (1) (d) read wit nesses 5(1)(c) of The Prevention of corrup tion of CorruptionAct is not attracted on the proved facts. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted merely by reason of the fact that the explanation tendered by the accused is reasonable and probable. it must further be shown that the explanations are supported by proof, the presumption createdby the provision can also be held to be discharged merely by reasons of the facts that the Explanation offered by th accused is unreasonable and probable; it must also be shown, that the said explanation is a true one. Unless there fore, the Explanation is supported by evidence, the presumptions created by section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot be held not be discharged simply by reason Of the fact, that t he explanation offered is reasonable or probable. It must further been shown that th e explanation was a true One. Unless, there fore , the explanation is supported y proof, presumption created under the provision could not be saidto be rebutted.

The appellant was a private Devasthan or a public religious trust. There was a saint endowed with spiritual powers by the name of Sakharam Maharaj at Amalner. The deity installed in the temple was intended by the Founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public: (1) In order to facilitate worship by the public, the founder also intended that regular Bhajan, Kirtan and worship shall be maintained and annual ceremonies and processions for pilgrimage shall be conducted by the saints in succession nominated by the reigning saint. (2) More than a century ago the temple in its own name was recipient of land by Royal grant and the same has been managed by the Saints and the Adhikaris or the disciples who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of the property; (3) In the absence of anything to the contrary of a convincing nature, a grant by the Government in favour of the temple describing the property to be in charge of a manager leads to an inescapable inference that the property is a public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. The Sanad being an ancient Royal grant was a very important piece of evidence to show that though Sakharamkar, the Chairman of the Sansthan, had already been succeeded by Guru Govindbuwa and the latter by Balkrishnabuwa, the land had been held in the year 1860 61 in the name Of the Devasthan. In accordance with this theory, it has been held that when property is dedicated for the worship of a family idol, it is a private and not a public endowment, as the persons who are entitled to worship at the shrine of the deity can only be the members of the family, and that is an ascertained group of individuals. Distinguishing the decision of the Privy Council in Bahu Bhagwan Din vs Gir Har Saroon on the ground that the properties in that case were granted not in favour to an idol but in favour Of one Daryao Gir who was maintaining a temple and to his heirs in perpetuity, this Court further held in that decision: "But, in the present case, the endowment was in favour o the idol itself, and the point for decision is whether it was private or public endowment. The consciousness of the constituted attorney about the nature of the trust on documentary evidence, if any, the object and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner inwhich the property had long been used by the Public, the contribution of the public to all intents and purposes as a matter of right without the least interference or restriction from the temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship by way of grants from the state of gifts from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of trust, the nature, of devolution of the properties, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is not a private or a private religious endowment. To sum up from the documentary and oral evidence produced, the following features are present in the instant case: (i) The deity erected in the Temple was intended to be continuously worshipped for more than a decade as a public temple; (ii) In accordance With this theory it has also been held by the Privy council that when the property was dedicated for worship of an idol, there is absolutely no evidence in this case about dedication to the public or public user of the Temple as a whole. (iii) Absence of any evidence in the long history of the institution to warrant that it had any appearance of, or that it was ever treated as a private property. While each case of endowment as to its character depends on the particular history.

The Income tax Officer issued a recovery certificate to the Additional Collector of Bombay against the petitioner under section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 for the recovery of the demand certified under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876. The petitioner challenged the validity of the recovery certificate on the ground that it was violative of article 22(1) and (2), article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioner: (i) that section 46 (2) is violative of articles 19(1)(f) and 21 of the constitution; (ii) that the provisions of all the State laws are mutatis mutandis to be read into section 46, (2); (iii) that sections 13 and 14 of Bombay City Act, 1879 under which the warrant of arrest was issued by the Additional collector is void under article 13(1), (3) and article 14; (iv) that in view of section 46 of the Income tax Officers issuing the recovery certificates to the Income Tax Officer, the machinery for the collection of arrears of land revenue should be framed on a uniform all India basis, for to the Union all defaulters who may not pay up the Union demand are similarly situated; but the Indian Incometax Act by section 46 has been amended and the warrant is issued on the 7th June 1955, that is to say, long after the amendment of section 13, the Collector, on receipt of the certificate from the Incometax Officer, has to proceed to recover the certified amount as if it were an arrear of land Revenue; (v) that s.46(2), which authorises the Collectors in different States to adopt machinery which differs from State to State, so that defaulters are treated differently in different states, can it be said to be unreasonable for the Union to adopt, for the purpose of recovering its public demand from defaulters of each State, the same mode of recovery (1) ; , 157. The grouping of income tax defaulters into separate categories or classes Statewise is certainly a territorial classification which is based on an intelligible differentia and the subjection, for, the purposes of the Recovery of the certified demand, of each such class of defaulter to the same coercive process devised by their own State, on a consideration of local needs, for recovery of their own public demands, cannot be regarded as bereft of a reasonable nexus or correlation between the basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Indian income tax Act any more than it can be so regarded with respect to the respective State laws. HELD: (1)(a) The Income tax officer may forward to the Collector a certificate under his signature specifying the amount of arrears due from an assessee and the Collector with the power to apply either of the two methods, that was to say he is to adopt the procedure prescribed by the appropriate law of his State for the Recovery Of its public demands. [157 B C] (b) The provisions of sections 13(2)(a), 13(4), 14(5), 15(6), 16(7), 17(8), 18(9), 19(10), 20, 21 and 22 of the Act do not make any distinction between State and State laws on the one hand and State law on the other. [158 F G] (2)(b) It is a well settled principle of interpretation that where two interpretations are possible, the one which favours an interpretation should be preferred to the former.

Section 4 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, a thika tenant shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be liable to ejectment from his holding on one or more of the specified grounds and not otherwise. Section 5 provided that where any decree or order for recovery of possession of any holding from a thikika tenant has been made before the date of commencement of this Ordinance but the ' possession of such holding has not been recovered from the thika tenants by the execution of such decree or orders, the Court by which the decree or the order was made may, if it is of opinion that the decree was not in conformity with any provision of this law other than sub section (1) of section 5 or section 27, rescind or vary the decree and order in such manner as the court may think fit for the purpose of giving effect to such provision and a decree or an order so varied by any Court shall be transferred by such Court to the Controller for execution under this Act as if it were an order made under and in accordance with the provisions contained in this Act. Section 29 provides that: "If, at any time between the commencement of the West Bengal Thika (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, a decree has been passed for the recovery of Possession of any land and for other relief, if any, and delivery of possession has not already been given, then on application made in this behalf by the person against whom the decree is passed, within three months of the commencement Of this Ordinance, the court which or the Controller who passed the decree shall decide (after hearing the parties and after taking fresh evidence if necessary) whether the person is a thukika tenant within the meaning of the said Act as amended by this Ordinance. " The question for consideration in this appeal was whether the respondent No. 1 was entitled to the benefit of section 4(2)(b) of the Act as it was finally amended by an Act of 1953. Held, that sections 4 and 5 being prospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the landlord had to establish the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3 in order to succeed.

The appellant was working as a Bench Secretaries Grade I in the Government of Uttar Pradesh. The pay scale recommended by the Pay Commission was Rs.1600 2950 to both the grades of Bench Secretaries with effect from January 1, 1986. The recommendation of the Pay Rationalisation Committee was accepted by the State Government on July 2, 1976. Thereafter, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated July 6, 1985. The High Court held that it would be violative of the constitutional right of equal pay for equal work and directed that all Bench Secretaries irrespective of their grades should be given the same scale of pay which is being given to Superintendents or the Section Officers. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of "equal pay for Equal work" has to be construed in the first place. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value Judgment of the administrative authorities who are charge with fixing the pay scales has tobe left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [310F G] 1.2 In comparison to Bench Secretaries, the Section Officer of the secretariat has to bear more responsibilities in their Section and have to control over its subordinates. Therefore, the responsibilities of the two posts cannot be said to be equal. Keeping in view the present scale of Pay, the nature of duties and responsibilities and the fact that every Honble Judge will have one Private Secretary in the scale of Rs.500 1,000 we feel that the Bench Secretaries may do the same work, but their quality of work may differ. Under the rules framed by the Chief Justice of the High Courts, Bench Secretaries grade I are selected by a Selection Committee. The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay scale and that merit will be evaluated by a competent authority. [309H; 310A B] 1:3 In comparison with Bench Secretaries of Grade I, the section Officers of the Secretariat have to bear greater responsibilities in its Section and had to control control over their subordinates. Under these rules, they are selected through a Selection committee. The Rules thus make it clear that this decision of ours shall not affect the Bench Secretary Secretaries to get that pay scale accordingly with effectfrom January 1. 1986. [334C D] 1 :4 In comparison, to Bench Stenographers Grade I and Group II PG NO 298, the High court has completely overlooked the criterion provided under the Rules The merit governs the grant of higher pay scales and that merits will be appreciated by a Competent authority. The classification made under the rules, therefore, cannot be held to be violative Of the right to have equal pay scale for equal Work. [313E F] 1.:5 In comparison To Bench Secretaries Rs.400 750 for Bench Secretaries and Rs. 500 1,500 to Section Officers are in a higher payscale than Bench SecretariesGrade II.

Section 127A of the Municipalities Act, 1961 provides that for the purpose of taxation, the Special Area Development Authority shall have the powers which a Municipal Corporation or a Municipal Council has under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 or the Madhya Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act. 1961, as the case may be, under the M.P. Municipalities Act and the Municipal Corporation, Notified Area Committee or a Panchayat, as defined in section 2(2) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, or any other law for the time being in force. Section 135 of the Municipal Corporations Act provides that the property tax shall not be leviable inter alia on "buildings and lands owned by or vesting in the Union Government". The first contention of the Attorney General is that assuming that section 127A was inserted in its present form in section 69, could be invoked for levying the property taxes, respondent 1 cannot impose that tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of the aforesaid Acts, respectively. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The power conferred by the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act on the Union government to regulate and develop the Coal mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources is therefore not in conflict with the power conferred under section 69(d). It was held by this Court that the legislative power of the State Legislature under Entry 24, List II, was eroded only to the extent to which control was assumed by the Union Parliament pursuant to the declaration made by the Parliament in respect of a declared industry and that the field occupied by such enactment was the measure of the erosion of the legislative competence of the state legislature. It was contended on behalf of 23 the sugar undertakings that since sugar is a declared Industry under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951, Parliament alone was competent to pass a law on the subject and the State legislature had no competence to pass the impugned Act by reason of Entry 52, List I read with Entry 24 of List II. The property tax is imposed by respondent 1 under section 127 A of the Municipality Act and section 135 of Municipal Corporation Corporation Act also provides that: (a) for the purposes of taxation the Special Areas Development Authority undertakes the functions under clause (v) or clause (vi) of section 68 cease to exercise the powers and perform the function and duties which the Special area Development Authority is competent to exercise and perform under the Act of 1973; (b) for purposes of clauses (v), (vi), (vii), (viii), (ix), (x), (xi), (xii), (xiii), (xiv), (xv), (xvi), (xvii), (xviii), (xix), (xx), (xxx), (xxi), (xxii), (xxiii), (xxiv), (xxv), (xxvi), (xxvii) and (xxviii), of section 69. The power to impose the property Tax on lands and buildings is therefore, not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section69(d) of Act 1973. [23C D] (2) The State Legislature had no power to regulate or develop the coal mines so that to ensure fair utilisation of Coal resources. The paramount purpose behind the declaration contained in section 1(2), Mines and Mineral (Regulation & Development) Ordinance, 1957 was not in no way defeated by legitimate exercise by taxing power Under section 69 of the Act. It is held by the majority speaking through one of us, Desai J., held that the State Government had waived its power of taxation by that agreement and, therefore, the imposition of property tax was invalid. [24D E] (3) The legislative power conferred on the State Legislatures to impose property tax on lands or buildings is thus not in conformity with the powers conferred by section 69 (d).

The appellant was granted a lease of the land in question for a period exceeding one year. The lease was for a term exceeding one years and it was not enforceable against the Government, according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The Board of Revenue passed an order on December 27, 1955 declaring that the lease had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that as the lease was in respect of a period beyond one year, it was liable to be terminated only in accordance with that proviso by giving three months ' notice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words " such rights" in the third proviso had reference to the rights created after July 1 1945, mentioned in the previous proviso and on that construction, the lease in favour of the appellants could only be terminated in accordance With that proviso. Held: (i) The words "such right" in section 20 (1) are two fold, namely, (a) that all rights created before the notified date but after July1, 1945 for a periods exceeding one month would also be valid and enforceable by the Government against the person in whose favour such right had been created; and (b) that rights created prior to July1 1945, are only voidable at the instance of the Government and that being the position, the Government must do some overt act to terminate the transaction. In other words, the true meaning of the second Proviso is said to be that rights acquired after July I 1945, were only voidable when it relates to the private land of the landholder within the meaning of section 3, clause (10), of the Estates Land Act, and (ii) such rights, however, may be determined under the third provisos if it is in the public interest to do so and in such cases, compensation will be payable under section 20.
